review.headline: The restage put the conclusion ahead of its premises. The definition (4.a, t=386s) and the set-equal algebra (4.c-4.e) now come before any hold where Qd and Qs are read at a price, compared, and tied to specific frustrated people. That machinery first appears at 5.a/5.b (t=416-433s), after Exercise Q1. The 386s discovery act does not supply those premises by other means. Its prices move because people enter, which is B5's "number of buyers/sellers" shifter, and no queue ring or unsold box appears anywhere in it. The market also settles about 18 times with no remark before the 18th settle is called equilibrium. The frame 4.a needs already exists as the last held frame of the lesson (5.h.iii, t=546s). It shows the plaza, the combined graph, P=$4, Qd=Qs=6, and the definition under the title "Would anyone gain by changing?".

findings.title: Dependency ledger: L3-L7 are used at 4.a/4.b but first established at 5.a-5.h
findings.claim: My refined chain is below. L0: a trade happens iff MC<=P<=MB, and the price splits the gain. L1: buyers compete with buyers and bid up; sellers compete with sellers and cut. L2: one price, because a buyer who sees a cheaper seller switches. L3: horizontal read, where Qd(P) is the count of units with MB>=P and Qs(P) the count with MC<=P. L4: at a candidate P, compare them to get the gap. L5: the gap is specific people who are willing at P and unserved or unsold. L6: those people have a private profitable deviation with a direction. L7: the rest point is no frustrated person, which is the same as Qd=Qs. L8: Qd=Qs is the crossing. L9: the crossing is where the equations are set equal. L10: any other P self-corrects. Links L0-L2 and the miniature of L6 are established early and well. L0 is at 2.a-2.b, L1 at 2.c and 3.a.seller.cut, L2 at 3.a.switch.options (t=63s), and L6 at 2.c.accepted. L3, L4, L5 and L7 are first needed at 4.a and 4.b. The notes prose at 4.a asks "What if quantity demanded was equal to quantity supplied?", and the "Qd=Qs=6" readout at 4.b needs the same links. They are first established at 5.a (the aggregate plug-in with the gold gap segment, t=416-430s), 5.b (unwilling people dimmed, willing-but-unserved buyers ringed, t=433s), and 5.d.i (unsold boxes). L7 is never argued. It is only co-displayed at the ends of 5.c and 5.g and at 5.h.iii. L8 gets one fade at 4.b. L10, together with the 5.h tests, is the evidence for L7, and it arrives 145s of motion and one exercise after L7 was asserted and assessed.
findings.evidence: In 03_Equilibrium.py:1273 the first Q_d/Q_s glyph of the episode appears, at 4.b. Lines 1569-1591 compute willing_buyers, willing_sellers and queued and do the dimming, and they sit inside the deviation loop only. Lines 1642-1644 hold the shortage and excess cards. Before 4.b the side panels are read only vertically, with one buyer's MB guide set against per-seller required prices (frames 27_3_a_growth_S2_r25_b0_options.jpg and 30_3_a_growth_B6_declined.jpg). Frame 34_4_a.jpg shows no Qd, no Qs, no count, and no distinction between willing and unwilling nontraders. The present.json stop counts give 143 of 225 stops and 386 of 547s before 4.a, 1 stop for 4.a, and 1 stop for 4.b.
findings.why_it_matters: A first-year student reaches the definition holding only "things stopped moving." The B1/B2 tools they actually own are plugging a price into a curve and reading a quantity. The B2 storyboard's price-tracker and Q_s readout idiom is the example. Those tools are not invoked until after the concept has been named, solved for algebraically, and exercised. At that point equilibrium is a word attached to a stillness, not the answer to a comparison the student could run.
findings.fix_sketch: Reorder existing assets so that L3-L6 precede L7-L9. Keep 2.a-2.c and a compressed arrival sequence through to 3.b, with the settle left unnamed. Then run 4.b with the plaza kept on screen. Run the toy deviations 5.b-5.c at $3 and 5.d.i-5.g at $6, followed by the 5.h tests at $4. Put the definition on the existing 5.h.iii frame. Then run the 4.c-4.e algebra as "find the P where the gap is zero," then Q1, then the 5.a/5.d aggregate plug-ins as the worked example for Q2. This requires splitting the `for test_price` loop around lines 1480-1890 into an aggregate-calculation half and a toy-return half. That is a refactor and needs no new animation.

findings.title: 4.a asserts "no one wants to change" but builds no bridge to Qd=Qs; the bridge frame is 5.h.iii
findings.claim: At 4.a the screen shows six pairs, four idle buyers, four idle sellers, and the card "Equilibrium is where no one wants to change." A gold arrow points at a dashed $4 marker on the supply panel. So the sentence is about people while the arrow points at a number. The on-screen card is also not the card in the notes. It dropped the Qd=Qs clause. Nothing on the frame tells a student why the eight idle people do not want to change. The idle sellers still post $5, $5, $6 and $6, so there is not yet one visible price either. The test that would justify the sentence carries the title "Would anyone gain by changing?", and that test runs at 5.h (t=531-546s). The frame that co-displays meanings (a) and (b) is the last held frame of the lesson, before the exercise card.
findings.evidence: In 03_Equilibrium.py:1212-1214 the card text is "Equilibrium is where no one wants to change." 01_Notes.md:67 reads "The price and quantity at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded — where no one wants to change." The arrow target is posted_marks[first_seller] (py:1216-1219). Compare frame 34_4_a.jpg with frame 65_5_h_iii.jpg. Taylor's original concept in Bx_Equilibrium_Video.typ placed the switching test at the naming of equilibrium: "this settling down where no one wants to move is equilibrium... first not everyone will buy and sell... then maybe show what happens if someone tries to switch, that there's no better option for them, that this is true for everyone."
findings.why_it_matters: Idle buyers look frustrated by default, because they came to buy and have nothing. Unless they are shown as unwilling at $4, which the existing 5.b dimming does, the definition reads as false or vacuous to a careful student. The a<->b equivalence is the economics of the whole lesson, and it is left entirely to improvisation over a frame that does not support it.
findings.fix_sketch: The smallest version reuses two existing blocks. (1) Restore the two-clause card from the notes, which is a text change. (2) Run the existing willing/unwilling treatment at P=$4 just before the card, as a first "What happens at $4?" pass of the deviation block (py:1569-1650). Six lit buyers and six lit sellers are all paired, so there are zero rings and zero boxes. Then run the $3 pass with four rings and the $6 pass with seven boxes as its contrasts. (3) Move the 5.h.i and 5.h.ii tests to directly follow that $4 pass.

findings.title: The discovery act moves prices by entry, not by disequilibrium at a fixed population
findings.claim: From 3.a.entry to 3.b the price path is $6.25 -> $5.50 -> $6.25 -> $4.50/$6.25 -> ... -> $4. Every leg is caused by a new arrival shifting demand or supply. 01_Notes.md:45 says as much: "add another buyer... the price creeps up. Add another seller and the pressure runs the other way." That is B5.1's "number of buyers / number of sellers" shifter, taught 14 times before equilibrium has a name. Each `.settled` hold is already an equilibrium of a smaller market, so the student sees about 18 rest points with no remark. The rest point at 4.a is distinguished only by Taylor ceasing to add people. The ED handoff (02_Storyboard.md item 3) justified the restage as "phenomena before names." Its proposal was that queues and leftover units would appear unlabeled during discovery. That was not implemented, and no ring or box exists for waiting buyers or unsold units anywhere before line 1210. So the phenomenon that act 5 names is never seen in act 3. The only fixed-population runs that start from a wrong price are 5.c and 5.g.
findings.evidence: Frames 19_3_a_two_pairs.jpg ($5.50 for both), 21_3_a_excluded.jpg ($6.25), 29_3_a_growth_S2_settled.jpg, and 33_3_b.jpg. A grep for box, queue and ring below line 1210 returns only the deliberating buyer's ring and the option rings. B_Skillsheet.typ B5.1 lists "number of buyers" and "number of sellers" as shifters. 02_Storyboard.md:101 says "not a claim that every quarter-dollar path gives equality." In the 2x2 market any P in [4,6] clears, so the $5.50 is path noise. present.json shows 107 stops and 231s of motion in 3.a.growth.
findings.why_it_matters: During the longest act, the live question in a student's head is who gets paired and what the newcomer does. The question of why this price, for these people, never comes up. When act 5 asks that second question, it is a new question. It is not a recognition of something they already watched.
findings.fix_sketch: Keep emergence but change what emerges. Reach 10x10 quickly by cutting or montaging most of 3.a.growth, keeping at most B2 plus one declined buyer. Then let the 5.c run from $3 and the 5.g run from $6 be the discovery. Both already have a fixed cast, a monotone price path, visible frustrated people, and the combined graph alongside. Alternatively, keep the growth and add the unlabeled waiting rings and unsold boxes that the ED note proposed, reusing the 5.b and 5.d assets.

findings.title: Restage seams: connectives written for shortage -> excess -> rest point no longer follow
findings.claim: (1) 01_Notes.md:63 reads "Can there ever be a price that doesn't change? Yes. What if quantity demanded was equal to quantity supplied?" In the archive (line 77) this followed "So prices will rise with a shortage and lower with an excess," a sentence now moved to 5.h (Notes:159). At the new 4.a the question is answered by the screen before it is asked. Qd and Qs have not appeared in the episode. The conjecture "what if Qd=Qs?" also loses its motivation, which was a shortage at $3 and an excess at $6 implying something in between. (2) Notes:65 reads "In this way incentives push the price to the point where Qs = Qd." The phrase "this way" pointed at the two deviation stories, which now come later. (3) Notes:79 reads "There's one price that allows Qs to equal Qd. And that's where they intersect." It was written after students had seen two horizontal gaps. Now it is asserted cold, and frame 36_4_c.jpg already has a starred dot placed at the crossing. (4) Notes:105-107 contains a new stitch, "a bunch of [buyers] get together and insist on... $3," immediately followed by the old sentence "spinach sellers... decide to sell at $3." That gives two different agents for one price in consecutive sentences. In the old order $3 was a neutral candidate price. Now it needs a collusion story because P* is already known. (5) The Notes 5.c beat comment, "the motion from the 3.a run, now named," presupposes queues in 3.a that do not exist.
findings.evidence: _archive/01_Notes_pre_restage_2026-09-20.md:77-81 and 87, compared with 01_Notes.md:63-65, 79, 105-107, and the 5.c comment. 02_Storyboard.md ED handoff item 2 anticipated the 4.a split.
findings.why_it_matters: Taylor improvises, but these seams mark the points where the hold on screen offers nothing to improvise from. At each one the natural next sentence needs an object, such as a gap or a frustrated queue, that the animation has not yet produced.
findings.fix_sketch: This is mostly resolved by the reorder in finding 1. If the current order stays, there are two script-only changes. At 4.a, replace the rhetorical question with an audit of the frame: "who here would change?" At 5.a, present $3 as a neutral candidate price with the question "why not $3?", and drop the huddle.

findings.title: The b<->c bridge is one fade-in on a graph where the crossing is a flat overlap, followed by a jump to a different market
findings.claim: At 4.b the price line, the drop line, "P=$4" and "Qd=Qs=6" all fade in together (py:1279). Nothing varies. With this fixture the staircases coincide along Q=4..6 at $4, and the drop sits at the right end of the overlap. So "cross" is a segment, and "6" holds only when indifferent traders are counted (Storyboard:147-148). After 4s the toy graph is replaced by the aggregate lines, a different market that shares only P=$4. The crossing dot and the starred unknowns are pre-placed under the title "Where do supply and demand meet?" No hold ever sweeps a price line with live Qd and Qs readouts so that the gap is seen to close at the crossing. B2's storyboard already has that tracker idiom. During 5.c and 5.g the common-price readout is removed (Storyboard:198).
findings.evidence: Frames 35_4_b.jpg, 36_4_c.jpg, and 45_5_a.jpg, the last of which shows the gold gap segment at $3. 03_Equilibrium.py:1269-1281. B2_Supply/02_Storyboard.md:68 has the price tracker moving $4 -> $6 -> $3 -> $4 with Q_s attached.
findings.why_it_matters: "Equilibrium is where the curves cross" becomes a picture to memorize. It should be a consequence: the crossing is the only height at which the two horizontal reads agree.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a small new animation on the aggregate graph. Reuse the red guides and gold gap segment from 5.a on a tracker sweeping $3 -> $6 -> $4, with both readouts live, so the gap shrinks to zero at the crossing. Do this before 4.d, and it becomes the reason for setting the equations equal. Consider making one MB and one MC non-integer so that the toy crossing is a point.

findings.title: The d-bridge and notation: the worked algebra uses a bare Q, the Q1 card uses Qd and Qs, and the skill says "set Qd equal to Qs"
findings.claim: The 4.c-4.d work writes P=12-Q/5 and P=2+Q/20 and equates the right-hand sides. That equates heights at a common Q. The exercise card shown immediately afterwards writes P=12-Qd/2 and P=2+Qs/2. Subscripted equations first appear in worked form at 5.a, after Q1. The step "at equilibrium Qd=Qs, so call both Q" is never on screen. In the pre-restage order, students had already computed two different numbers, Qs=20 and Qd=45, at a single P. Collapsing those to one Q was then the visible content of the word equilibrium.
findings.evidence: 03_Equilibrium.py:1307-1314 uses plain Q, line 1454 is the Q1 card with Q_d and Q_s, and lines 1491-1494 are the subscripted copies inside the deviation loop. Frame 42_4_exercise.jpg. B_Skillsheet.typ B3.1 says "solve... by setting quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied."
findings.why_it_matters: In Q1 a student faces two equations in three symbols with no stated licence to merge Qd and Qs. The recipe works only by pattern-matching to the example, and that is exactly the recipe-without-reason feel Taylor is describing.
findings.fix_sketch: This is mostly a text change. Write the 4.c labels with Q_d and Q_s. Add one row, "Q_d = Q_s = Q*", before 4.d.collect. Or place the plug-in holds before the solve, as in finding 1.

findings.title: The spine question never gets a hold, and roughly two thirds of the stops do not serve it
findings.claim: The spine is stated in B2's closing line and again in Notes 1.b: is there a price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers want, and why would a market go there and stay? Beats 1.a and 1.b, the twin-curve recap and the floating price marked "?", are not in the animation, which goes from 0.a directly to 2.a. The on-screen titles run "Would they exchange?", then "What would Amanda-Grace gain?", then "Where do prices settle?". That last title is held for 332s. Several groups of holds do not serve the spine. 2.b.i-2.b.vi is the Expenditure/CS/Revenue/MC/PS/One-unit accounting, which is B1/B2 recap that serves B4. 3.a.two_pairs is the $5.50 hold with Gary's $0.50 gain. 3.a.excluded, 3.a.excluded.reason, 3.a, 3.a.lookout, 3.a.options and 3.a.chosen tell an allocation story. Nearly all of the 107 3.a.growth.* stops fall in the same category. 5.e is the surplus-versus-excess aside. The 4.c.i and 4.d.* holds serve only meaning (d).
findings.evidence: A grep of pause() and title() in 03_Equilibrium.py shows no 1.x pause, and the titles sit at lines 77, 351, 440, 1225, 1292, 1480 and 1893. B2_Supply/01_Notes.md:153. The present.json tallies.
findings.why_it_matters: Without the floating-price setup, Qd(P) and Qs(P) are not the active tools when the plaza opens. The plaza then reads as a new topic and not as the answer to B2's cliffhanger.
findings.fix_sketch: Add one hold before 2.a by reusing the 4.c aggregate axes. Show the two curves with a drifting price line and "?", then cut to the plaza. Collapse the 2.b accounting to one hold, since B4 will redo it. Treat most growth stops as skip-through.

findings.title: 2.c.iii is a free miniature of the a<->b bridge that goes unused
findings.claim: The bidding war is equilibrium in the small. At $4 two buyers want Molly's one unit, so Qd=2 and Qs=1. The price climbs in quarter-dollar steps and stops at $6.25, exactly where Gary drops out and Qd=1=Qs. The hold's caption reads "Gary: next bid $6.50 > MB $6." That is the individual half of the argument, given with no count. The title at that hold is "What would Amanda-Grace gain?"
findings.evidence: Storyboard rows 2.c.i-2.c.iii, 03_Equilibrium.py:351-427, and frame 11_2_c_iii.jpg, at t=51s.
findings.why_it_matters: It is the cheapest place to plant "the price moves while more people want in than there are units, and it stops when the counts match." Planted there, 4.a and 5.b become recognitions.
findings.fix_sketch: This needs script and caption changes only. Add a second caption line at 2.c.iii, such as "At $4: 2 want it, 1 unit. At $6.25: 1 wants it, 1 unit."

findings.title: The 5.h stability tests give the marginal-person reason, not the competition reason in the notes
findings.claim: 5.h.i tests an MB-$4 buyer against a $4.25 proposal and gives the refusal reason "$4.25 > MB $4." 5.h.ii tests an MC-$4 seller against a $3.75 offer. The four-way argument in Notes:63-65 rests on competition: "If a seller raised their price, they would lose all their business." The animation's reason would not apply to the seller paired with the MB-$8 buyer. A sharp student will ask why that seller cannot charge $5. The model's permitted moves (Sim/discovery.py, improvements()) do not include a matched seller raising the price, and the storyboard concedes this at lines 145-147.
findings.evidence: Frames 61_5_h_i_offer.jpg, 62_5_h_i.jpg and 63_5_h_ii.jpg. Storyboard row 5.h and the "Stopping is an exhaustive audit of permitted improvements" paragraph.
findings.why_it_matters: It leaves "no one wants to change" demonstrated only for the two people with zero surplus. Those are the least intuitive exemplars of being content.
findings.fix_sketch: Add one more test that reuses the same close-up. An inframarginal seller posts $4.25, the buyer walks to the hub, sees $4 elsewhere, and leaves, so the seller gains an unsold box. If the simulation cannot support that, handle it in the script.

what_works: 2.a.i, 2.b and 2.c.i through 2.c.accepted work. The dashed (contemplated) to solid (accepted) price grammar and the caption "Amanda-Grace gains $7-$4.25=$2.75" establish a private incentive and its direction, in one concrete instance, within the first 40s. This is L6 done right.
3.a.switch.options ("Would Amanda-Grace keep paying $6.25?") builds the one-price link before it is needed at 4.b. 3.a.seller.cut gives the mirrored seller-side incentive.

3.a.excluded and 3.a.excluded.reason, along with growth declines such as 30_3_a_growth_B6_declined.jpg ("Every offer exceeds this buyer's MB"), show that nontraders are out because of price versus MB and not because of bad luck. That is half of the a<->b bridge. It only needs gathering at 4.a.

Frames 46_5_b.jpg and 53_5_d_i.jpg are the best frames in the lesson. Unwilling people are dimmed, willing-but-unserved buyers are ringed, and unsold units are boxed. Each frame sits beside the staircase graph with separate Qs and Qd drops and the definition card. Here the gap is specific people.
5.g.production ("Would these sellers produce at $4?") shows Qs falling along the supply curve as the price falls, so the excess closes from both sides.

Frame 65_5_h_iii.jpg puts the plaza, the combined graph, P=$4, Qd=Qs=6, and the definition together under the title "Would anyone gain by changing?". This is the right definition frame. It is only in the wrong place.

In 4.c.i through 4.d.i, the colored equation copies travel from the graph labels into the working, and the red answers are carried back to the starred unknowns. The c<->d bridge is the best built of the three bridges.
The storyboard is candid about what the toy shows versus what it proves (lines 101 and 145-150), and it keeps the toy's six units distinct from the aggregate 40,000 lb.
open_questions: How much class time did 3.a.growth take today? If Taylor skipped through most of its 107 stops, the emergence case is stronger than the motion-time share of 231 of 547s suggests.
Skill B3.1, bullet 3, says quantity exchanged is min(Qd,Qs). It is implicit at 5.b, with four trades when Qs=4, but it is never labeled on screen. Is it meant to live in B3 or in B4's price controls?

Is the flat overlap on Q=4..6 at $4, with two zero-gain pairs, a deliberate fixture choice made for B4's marginal-unit discussion? Or is it incidental, and free to be perturbed so that the toy crossing is a point?

The case for the current order rests on naming the phenomenon after students have seen it, on the memorable line that nobody told anyone to stop, and on the style guide's rule that abstractions are earned. I think that case holds under three conditions. First, the discovery is short enough that "why here?" is still a live question at 4.a. Second, the discovery displays the same observables that the definition uses: one price line, willing versus unwilling people, and rings and boxes. Third, the named rest point is reached with a fixed cast. The current build meets none of the three. The runs at 5.c and 5.g meet all three. Would Taylor accept those two runs as the discovery?

Does Taylor want the star-lands-where-the-market-settled payoff? At present the star lands on a dot pre-placed at 4.c, in a different market that shares only P=$4. The payoff would be real only if the algebra were run on a linearization of the toy, or if the aggregate market were shown to settle.

verdicts.title: Dependency ledger: L3-L7 are used at 4.a/4.b but first established at 5.a-5.h
verdicts.note:
The facts check out. The first Q_d/Q_s glyph in 03_Equilibrium.py is at line 1273 (4.b); a grep finds none earlier. willing_buyers, willing_sellers, queued and the dimming sit at py:1569-1611, inside the `for test_price in (3, 6)` loop that starts at py:1475. The shortage and excess cards are at py:1642-1644. In present.json, 4.a is stop index 144 of 225 (143 if the unnamed t=0 stop is excluded), at t=386.5s. Frame 34_4_a.jpg shows no count, no Qd/Qs, and no willing/unwilling distinction.

Three parts are overstated.
1. L5 is not absent before 4.a for buyers. Six `.declined` holds (B2, B3, B6, B7, B8, B9) carry the caption 'Every offer exceeds this buyer's MB' (frame 30), and 3.a.excluded.reason covers Gary. What is missing is the gathering of those facts into a count, and any equivalent for idle sellers.
2. 'L7 is never argued' is too strong. 5.h runs two explicit tests under the title 'Would anyone gain by changing?', and 5.g.production argues why the high-cost sellers leave.
3. The pre-restage notes are not a clean 'logical order' baseline. In that version the simulation was a separate companion video (archive line 19: 'In a companion video, we'll run a little fun simulation') and the episode was graph-only. The build-then-deviate order is Taylor's own direction (archive :185: 'start with the small number of players first, building up equilibrium, then do the deviations animations on the back end'). It also matches style guide section 9 line 559, the 'phenomenon-first christening pattern'.

'A refactor that needs no new animation' understates the work. The 5.c run strips the rings, the dimming, the common price line and the readouts (py:1666-1667 and 1788-1790; frame 50). Frame 65 has the four unwilling buyers at full brightness. Putting the definition on 5.h.iii would not give the full willing/unwilling picture without new work.

The reorder also has a cost the reviewer did not count. Q1 now comes at 411s of motion and would move past about 520s, so the first student activity of the class lands near the end.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Before the definition, the algebra and Q1, no hold reads a market-level quantity at a price or compares Qd with Qs. The only market-level object students have seen is per-seller posted-price dashes. Individual exclusion by price (the buyer side of L5) is shown repeatedly in act 3, but it is never aggregated into a count, and the idle sellers are never explained. The diagnosis is core. The prescription should be the smaller one: insert a horizontal read and a willing/unwilling pass at $4 before the card. A wholesale reorder undoes Taylor's own sequencing and pushes Q1 late.

verdicts.title: 4.a asserts "no one wants to change" but builds no bridge to Qd=Qs; the bridge frame is 5.h.iii
verdicts.note:
The card text at py:1213 is 'Equilibrium is where no one wants to change.' Notes:67 has the two-clause definition. The arrow targets posted_marks[first_seller] on the supply panel (py:1216-1219), and frame 34 shows exactly that. Idle sellers' dashed posted prices sit at $5 and $6 on the right-hand columns of frame 34. Frame 65 does co-display the plaza, the unit graph, P=$4, Qd=Qs=6 and the card under the title 'Would anyone gain by changing?'. The core claim stands.

Two corrections.
1. The Bx_Equilibrium_Video.typ quotation is stitched with ellipses across about 25 lines. In the original, the naming happens on the settle, exactly as 4.a does now ('eventually things settle down / this settling down where no one wants to move is equilibrium'). It is followed immediately by 'first not everyone will buy and sell / some will be unhighlighted'. The 'someone tries to switch' test comes only after the multi-unit extension and the graph overlay. The original concept therefore supports dimming the non-traders at the naming point, which is the reviewer's fix step 2. It does not support moving the 5.h tests up to the naming.
2. Frame 65 is not a complete bridge frame. py:1788-1790 resets every body to full opacity before the adjustment run, and only the withdrawn sellers are re-dimmed at 5.g.production (py:1878 onward). At 5.h.iii the four unwilling buyers (MB 3, 3, 2, 2) are as bright as the traders.

The short card also matches the episode thesis at 0.a and Notes:3 ('Equilibrium: when no one wants to change'). Dropping the second clause looks deliberate, not an accident.
verdicts.corrected_claim: 4.a names equilibrium on a frame that gives no visual reason the eight idle people are content. The idle sellers visibly post $5 and $6 with no buyers, and the arrow points at a price marker, not at people. The cheapest repair that fits Taylor's original concept ('some will be unhighlighted') is to run the existing willing/unwilling dimming at $4 before the card and to restore the Qd=Qs clause. The 5.h.iii frame needs the same buyer dimming before it can serve as the bridge.

verdicts.title: The discovery act moves prices by entry, not by disequilibrium at a fixed population
verdicts.note:
The central dichotomy is wrong as stated. Each arrival is a shock, and it is followed by fixed-cast competitive adjustment. That adjustment takes most of the act's motion time.

The per-arrival tallies in present.json show this. S2's arrival alone is 47 stops, 53 rounds and 119s. It is a fixed 4x4 cast descending from about $5.50 (frame 27, r25) to $4/$4.25 (frame 29, S2.settled, t=312). B2 takes 20 stops and 43s. Together they are 162 of the 231 growth seconds. After t=312 the remaining 12 arrivals take 73s and barely move anything. Six of the seven later buyers simply decline, and four of the seven later sellers have a single stop. 'B5's shifter taught 14 times' is therefore rhetoric. About five arrivals move the price at all, and students have not met B5 yet.

'The phenomenon that act 5 names is never seen in act 3' is refuted by frame 18 (3.a.seller.cut). Molly posts $6.25 with no buyer, Amanda-Grace is unmatched, and the on-screen question is 'Would Molly lower her price?'. Frame 11 (2.c) shows two buyers for one unit. The reviewer's own finding 8 calls that equilibrium in miniature. The grep claim is also slightly off, because gary_ring at py:944 rings an excluded buyer who is waiting.

What is true: the queue and leftover markers promised by Notes:48 and by ED item 3 do not exist before py:1574. There is no market-level count and no common price line in act 3. Roughly 18 settles go unremarked (14 `.settled` plus 2.c.iii, two_pairs, excluded and chosen). The market is already at about $4 by t=312, so 3.b looks the same as S2.settled.

The fix sketch is wrong about 5.c. During the 5.c run, the rings are faded (py:1667), the dimming is reset (py:1788-1790), and the price line and Qd/Qs readouts are removed (Storyboard:198). Frame 50 shows a bare plaza. 5.c does not already have 'visible frustrated people'. Only 5.g keeps its boxes.

Cutting or montaging 3.a.growth also collides with Taylor's explicit choice of sequential arrivals with deliberation (Storyboard:204-205; archive :183).
verdicts.corrected_claim: Act 3 does show disequilibrium dynamics at a fixed cast: an unsold seller cutting, buyers outbidding, and S2's 53-round descent. It never renders them in the observables the definition uses, which are counts of people wanting versus units available, one price line, and marked waiting buyers or unsold units. The act also spends 73s after the price has effectively reached $4 on arrivals that change nothing. The problem is legibility and pacing of the adjustment. The adjustment itself is present.

verdicts.title: Restage seams: connectives written for shortage -> excess -> rest point no longer follow
verdicts.note:
Every line citation checks out: archive:77 against Notes:63 and 159, Notes:65, Notes:79, Notes:105-107, and the 5.c beat comment at Notes:120.

Seam 5 is stronger than the reviewer states. Notes:48, the 3.a beat comment, itself reads 'queues and leftover units appear but stay unlabeled'. The notes and the animation therefore disagree outright.

Three points weaken the finding.
1. Taylor says the notes are prep material, not a script. These seams are symptoms of finding 1, not an independent 'major' defect. The reviewer half-concedes this.
2. Seam 4 reads the huddle line (Notes:105) as a patch forced on the text because P* is already known. It is a deliberate insertion with a designed payoff at Notes:165: 'a whole side of the market teamed up to move the price, and it still didn't hold. Someone always found it worthwhile to break ranks.' Dropping the huddle discards that payoff. The real seam is only the unedited old sentence at Notes:107, which makes sellers the agent. The animation has no huddle at all, and its title is simply 'What happens at $3?'.
3. The reviewer attributes the restage to ED's 'phenomena before names'. ED item 3 is marked 'Proposal pending with Taylor'. The order itself came from Taylor (archive :185).
verdicts.corrected_claim: The notes carry leftover connectives from the old order at lines 63, 65, 79 and 107. Notes:48 and Notes:120 also promise queue and leftover visuals in act 3 that the animation never built. Treat these as diagnostic evidence for finding 1 at minor severity. Keep the huddle and its break-ranks payoff, and fix only the agent clash at Notes:107.

verdicts.title: The b<->c bridge is one fade-in on a graph where the crossing is a flat overlap, followed by a jump to a different market
verdicts.note:
Confirmed facts:
- py:1279 fades the price line, the drop, 'P=$4' and 'Qd=Qs=6' in together.
- Frame 35 shows the staircases coinciding on Q=4..6 at $4, with the drop at 6.
- 4.b to 4.c is 4s of motion (390.8 to 394.8).
- Frame 36 has the dot and the dashed guides pre-placed with 'P*=?' and 'Q*=?'.
- Storyboard:198 removes the common-price readout during the runs.

Two things were missed or overstated.
1. The strongest precedent is B2's closing beat (B2 storyboard line 143), not B2:68. That beat has a shared red price line moving across side-by-side demand and supply, with Q_d and Q_s labels sliding in opposite directions. Students saw the sweep at the end of last class, and B3 never picks it up. This makes the fix cheaper, because the asset exists. It also makes the absence inside B3 more conspicuous.
2. The pre-placed dot follows the B1/B2 'unknown-before-answer' convention (Storyboard:163-164). That is a design choice, not an oversight.

The suggestion to make one MB non-integer is overreach, for three reasons. The simulation requires values on the quarter-dollar grid (discovery.py:93). The fixture's outcome is asserted at py:1204-1205. The flat segment supplies the MB-$4 and MC-$4 marginal participants that both 5.h tests depend on.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Inside B3, the step from Qd=Qs to the crossing is a single simultaneous fade on a graph where the crossing is a two-unit flat segment. The lesson then jumps after 4s to a different market. Nothing varies the price with both readouts live, even though B2's closing beat did exactly that. Reuse the B2 closing tracker on the 4.c axes before the equations are set equal, and leave the fixture alone.

verdicts.title: The d-bridge and notation: the worked algebra uses a bare Q, the Q1 card uses Qd and Qs, and the skill says "set Qd equal to Qs"
verdicts.note:
py:1307-1314 writes a bare Q. Frame 42 and Exercise_B3.typ use Q_d and Q_s. py:1491-1494 uses the subscripted forms only inside the deviation loop. B_Skillsheet B3.1 says 'by setting quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied'.

The finding is stronger than stated. B2 wrote its supply equation with the subscript throughout, as P=2+Q_s/10 (B2 storyboard lines 34, 40, 71 and 119). B3's bare Q at 4.c is a regression from the notation students used last class. Frame 45 (5.a) also shows the clash on a single screen: the graph labels read P=12-Q/5 and P=2+Q/20, while the working beside them reads Q_s and Q_d.

One mitigating detail is that 4.b displays 'Qd=Qs=6' 4s of motion before 4.c, so the identity is on screen nearby. It is never carried into the algebra as the licence to merge the two symbols.

verdicts.title: The spine question never gets a hold, and roughly two thirds of the stops do not serve it
verdicts.note:
The first half is confirmed. The pause list goes from 0.a (py:70) to 2.a (py:119) with no 1.x pause. Storyboard row 2.a folds 'Notes 1.a/2.a' together. 'Where do prices settle?' is held from t=54.5 to 386.5, which is 332s.

The reviewer missed that the floating-price question was staged as the closing animated beat of B2 (B2 storyboard line 143, 'What determines the price?', with a moving shared price line and Q_d/Q_s labels). The gap is that B3 does not re-open with it. It is not that the question was never staged.

The 'two thirds of stops' headline is stop-count rhetoric. 107 growth stops and 45 stops in 5.c/5.g are skip-pauses (Storyboard:182 'Each changed round has a skip pause'). The reviewer's own open question 1 concedes that the class-time share is unknown.

The finding is also internally inconsistent. Finding 1 credits 2.b with establishing L0 ('the price splits the gain'). what_works praises 3.a.excluded and the declines as 'half of the a<->b bridge'. This finding then lists the same holds as off-spine. The 2.b accounting is Taylor's verbatim direction (archive :181, 'use the price line in red to show what's going to the seller and the buyer, and expenditure, and cs and ps') and costs 11s. 'Collapse to one hold' is overreach.
verdicts.corrected_claim: B3's animation never re-poses B2's cliffhanger, the floating price with Qd and Qs read off both curves, before it cuts to the plaza. Plugging a price into a curve is therefore not an active tool when the plaza opens. Re-use B2's closing tracker as a 1.b hold. The stop-count argument should be dropped. The real pacing issue is the 73s after S2.settled and the single 332s title.

verdicts.title: 2.c.iii is a free miniature of the a<->b bridge that goes unused
verdicts.note:
Frame 11 verifies the state: Gary MB $6, Amanda-Grace MB $7, Molly MC $2, accepted price $6.25, caption 'Gary: next bid $6.50 > MB $6.', title 'What would Amanda-Grace gain?'. The bidding runs from $4 in quarter-dollar steps (Storyboard rows 2.c.i-2.c.iii) and stops exactly where the number of buyers wanting the unit falls to one.

This is an opportunity and not a defect, so 'minor' is the right severity. This finding, together with frame 18, contradicts finding 3's claim that act 3 never shows the phenomenon. The suggested caption is accurate for the fixture. At any price above $6 only Amanda-Grace wants the unit.

verdicts.title: The 5.h stability tests give the marginal-person reason, not the competition reason in the notes
verdicts.note:
Frames 61-63 verify the tests. 5.h.i uses an MB-$4 buyer paired with an MC-$3 seller, a $4.25 proposal and the refusal '$4.25 > MB $4', and leaves an unsold box beside the seller. 5.h.ii uses an MC-$4 seller, a $3.75 proposal and 'Would this seller accept?'. discovery.py improvements() (lines 46-64) permits only cuts by unmatched sellers and visits by buyers. A matched seller cannot raise. Storyboard:145-147 concedes the limit.

The fix needs a correction, because it does not work in this fixture. In the final state all six sellers with MC<=4 are matched at $4, and the idle sellers post $5 and $6 (frame 34). There is no open '$4 elsewhere' for the buyer to see. Under the outbid rule (discovery.py:58, offer = ask + step when the seller is occupied), a buyer facing a one-tick raise to $4.25 can only get $4.25 at an occupied seller, so she is indifferent. The competition story needs a two-tick raise, and that starts a displacement chain.

5.h.i is also already the notes' 'a seller who raises the price loses the business' shown on screen, via the unsold box. It just uses the one buyer for whom the reason is MB rather than alternatives.
verdicts.corrected_claim: 5.h shows stability only through the two zero-surplus marginal participants. The competition reason that covers inframarginal traders cannot be shown with a one-tick deviation under the current outbid rule and fixture. It needs a $4.50 raise plus a staged switch, or it should be carried in speech.

overreach: The headline 'the restage put the conclusion ahead of its premises' treats the pre-restage notes as the sound baseline. In that version the simulation was not in the episode at all. It was a 'companion video' (archive line 19). Both the build-then-deviate order and the sequential arrivals are Taylor's explicit directions (archive :185; Storyboard:204-205). They match style guide section 9's 'phenomenon-first christening pattern' and the original Bx concept, which names equilibrium on the settle.

The Bx_Equilibrium_Video.typ quotation is ellipsis-stitched. In the original, the switching test comes well after the naming, following the multi-unit extension and the graph overlay. What sits at the naming point is 'not everyone will buy and sell / some will be unhighlighted'.

Open question 4 and the fix in finding 3 assert that the 5.c and 5.g runs already display 'one price line, willing versus unwilling people, and rings and boxes'. They do not. The rings fade at py:1667, the dimming resets at py:1788-1790, and the common price readout is removed (Storyboard:198). Frame 50 (5.c.round13) is a bare plaza beside a graph with no Qd/Qs. Only 5.g keeps its boxes.

'B5's shifter taught 14 times before equilibrium has a name' is wrong. Only about five arrivals move any price. Six of the seven later buyers just decline, and four of the seven later sellers have a single stop. Students have not met B5, so the confusion is hypothetical. It could equally work as foreshadowing.

'Roughly two thirds of the stops do not serve it' counts skip-pauses as lesson content. It also contradicts the reviewer's own credit to 2.b (L0) and to 3.a.excluded and the declines (half of the a<->b bridge).
'Drop the huddle' ignores the designed payoff at Notes:165, that a whole side teamed up and someone still broke ranks.

'Make one MB non-integer so the toy crossing is a point' would break the quarter-dollar grid check (discovery.py:93), the asserted six-trades-at-$4 fixture (py:1204-1205), and the zero-gain marginal participants that both 5.h tests use.

The full reorder in finding 1 is described as a refactor needing 'no new animation'. It would require new dimming and ring work, because 5.h.iii and the runs lack them. It would also move Q1 from 411s to past 520s of motion, so the first student activity lands near the end of class. The reviewer never weighs that pacing cost.

Algebra before deviations has a rationale the reviewer does not mention. Taylor's planning note (archive :175) says 'use some math, find the price, set the price, and see if anyone switches... equilibrium is predictable and about deviation'. The current order follows that predict-then-perturb idea. Its weakness is that the prediction is made in a different market from the one perturbed, which the reviewer raises only as an open question.
missed: S2's arrival alone is 47 stops, 53 rounds and 119s. That is over half of 3.a.growth and the longest single stretch of the lesson. It is a fixed 4x4 cast grinding from about $5.50 to $4/$4.25 in quarter-dollar steps (frames 27 and 29). This is where a 'why here?' question dies. It is a pacing problem, and it is separate from the ordering of the beats.

The market is effectively at $4 by S2.settled (t=312, frame 29). The next 12 arrivals (73s, 35 stops) mostly decline or do nothing. The 3.b and 4.a 'settle' is visually the same as the one 73s earlier, so there is no climax for the definition to land on. The line 'trading gets calmer and calmer until prices stop' (Notes:57) has no matching visual.

Idle sellers are never explained. Buyers get `.lookout`, `.options` and `.declined` holds with a caption. S3, S6, S8 and S9 (MC 5, 6, 5, 6) each get a single `.settled` stop. At 4.a they sit posting their MC with no buyer (frame 34). They are the people on the frame who most obviously 'want to change', and nothing has said why they cannot.

The observables are stripped during the very runs meant to show adjustment. 5.c runs with no rings, no dimming, no price line and no Qd/Qs (frame 50; py:1666-1667 and 1788-1790). At 5.h.iii the unwilling buyers are undimmed while the unwilling sellers are dimmed (frame 65). The 'gap is specific people' idiom the reviewer praises in frames 46 and 53 lasts exactly one hold per deviation.

There is a notation clash on a single frame. At 5.a (frame 45) the graph labels read P=12-Q/5 and P=2+Q/20, while the working beside them uses Q_s and Q_d. B2 used Q_s in its equations throughout (B2 storyboard lines 34, 40, 71), so the bare Q in B3 is a regression.

B2's closing animated beat (B2 storyboard line 143) already is the two-curve floating-price tracker, with Q_d and Q_s moving in opposite directions. It is the natural asset both for a B3 1.b hold and for the gap-closing sweep before 4.d. The reviewer cited only the single-curve tracker at B2:68.

Notes:48, the 3.a beat comment, already specifies 'queues and leftover units appear but stay unlabeled'. The notes adopted the ED proposal and the animation did not build it. This is a concrete disagreement between the notes and the animation, and it counts for more than ED item 3, which was only 'pending'.

The toy and aggregate markets share only P=$4 (Storyboard:190-191). Every deviation is therefore computed in one market (20 versus 45) and enacted in another (4 versus 8), with a full fade to black between them at py:1561. Students must carry 'shortage' across a representation change twice. A horizontal read on the unit staircase at $3 and $6, before any aggregate algebra, would let the toy carry the concept by itself.

Skill B3.1 bullet 3, quantity exchanged = min(Qd, Qs), is on screen implicitly at 5.b (four trades when Qs=4) and never labelled. The reviewer left this as an open question. It is an assessed skill with no hold.

review.lens: Cognitive load and multimedia learning design (Sweller CLT; Mayer coherence/signaling/segmenting/pre-training/contiguity/redundancy; transient-information effect; Lowe & Schnotz salience vs. relevance; Tversky on animation)
review.headline: The lesson's thesis is a MARKET-level emergent fact (many prices collapse to one; Qd=Qs; nobody can do better), but the hold skeleton is spent almost entirely on INDIVIDUAL-level, isomorphic "is MB above the needed price?" comparisons: 3.a.* takes 128 of 224 named stops (57%) and 334 of 547 motion-seconds (61%), and one arrival alone (3.a.growth.S2) takes 47 stops / 119 s / 23 near-identical options->accepted pairs, while "name equilibrium" + "merge the curves" get 2 stops and 5.3 s. The emergent fact itself is never signaled where it happens: at 4.a the frame has no "$4" numeral, no trade count, no Qd=Qs, no price line on the Demand panel, and the 3D plaza physically cannot show "one price" because perspective puts equal prices at different screen heights; the frame that finally does show everything together (5.h.iii) arrives at t=546 of 547. Meanwhile the quantitative information that drives each decision lives on a side panel at ~11-15 px per $0.25 tick, while motion and screen-centre salience pull the eye to an unscaled, occluding plaza. Low-interactivity content is over-supported and over-segmented; high-interactivity content is under-supported and transient.

findings.title: Budget inversion: half the holds are one repeated micro-decision; the thesis gets two holds
findings.claim: From present.json (224 named stops, 547.3 s motion): first pair 3 stops/8.9 s (1.6%); accounting 6/11.2 s (2.0%); 3-person bidding 5/24.1 s (4.4%); small cast 2x2-3x3 18/98.9 s (18.1%); growth to 10x10 110 stops (49.1%)/235.1 s (43.0%); definition 4.a 1 stop/1.0 s; staircase merge 4.b 1 stop/4.3 s; equilibrium algebra 7/19.4 s (3.5%); shortage = 5 algebra stops/18.9 s + 18 plaza stops/30.7 s; excess = 5/18.9 s + 36/50.5 s; stability 6/16.1 s. Within growth: B2 arrival 20 stops/42.7 s (9 options pairs); S2 arrival 47 stops/119.4 s (23 options->accepted pairs, rounds r2...r53) = 21.8% of ALL motion in the episode; the remaining 12 arrivals total 43 stops/73 s and are mostly 'Every offer exceeds this buyer's MB'. Across the episode 49 .options + 40 .accepted + 6 .declined + 42 .roundN = 137 of 224 stops (61%) are the same two frame templates. The exercise and skill B3.1 assess: solve Q*,P* and plot; Qd,Qs at a price; shortage/excess and size; direction of adjustment; quantity exchanged = short side. The assessed algebra gets 17 stops (7.6%) / 57 s (10.5%). Nothing assesses the path of discovery.
findings.evidence: present.json stop list (e.g. 3.a.growth.S2.r2.b1.options t=197.9 ... 3.a.growth.S2.r53.b2.accepted t=311.9; 3.a.growth.S2.settled t=312.4); 03_Equilibrium.py:1129 and :1183 (a pause on every visible decision and every acceptance inside the loop); frames 27_3_a_growth_S2_r25_b0_options.jpg vs 28_..._accepted.jpg vs 26_3_a_growth_B2_r1_b4_options.jpg (visually interchangeable); contrast 2.c.ii->2.c.iii where seven quarter-dollar bids are compressed into ONE 13.9 s play (03_Equilibrium.py:392-427). Taylor's own design doc: Bx_Market_Animation/Market_Scene_Design.md:60 'Demonstrate one decision slowly, then compress the remaining visits.' Notes 3.a/3.b (01_Notes.md:48-57) ask for 'continuous action ... the trading gets calmer and calmer'.
findings.why_it_matters: A single buyer comparison has low element interactivity; students have it after 2-3 worked instances (2.c.i, 3.a.switch.options, 3.a.options). Continuing to present it as a fully worked, double-paused example ~45 more times is the redundancy/expertise-reversal pattern: it consumes attention and class minutes without adding schema, and it over-segments the one thing that must be seen as a gestalt (prices sliding down and stopping). Because Taylor improvises off the holds, 61% of the skeleton hands the lecturer nothing new to say; the talk is forced either to narrate trivia or to mash the advance key through 4 minutes of motion, which converts it into pure transient animation. The students leave with a vivid memory of 'dots walking to other dots' and a thin memory of why $4.
findings.fix_sketch: Script/flag-only first step: keep the six fully worked decisions up to 3.a.chosen, then in the growth loop gate the pauses at :1129 and :1183 off (or only for the newcomer's first decision) so each arrival has exactly one hold, the existing `.settled` (14 stops instead of 110). Second step (reuse of existing choreography): play each arrival's rounds in the compact 5.c/5.g 'changed-round' style (about 1.3 s per round, no hub walk per buyer) instead of the full survey choreography; or shorten S2 by choosing a seed/starting asks or a $0.50 tick so the fall from $6.25 to $4 takes ~8 cuts not 53 rounds. Reallocate the freed holds to 4.a/4.b (see next finding).

findings.title: The emergent outcome is not signaled at the moment it is named (4.a), and its cause is transient
findings.claim: At 4.a the title still asks 'Where do prices settle?' but the answer is not written anywhere: plaza price numerals were removed when the third seller arrived (storyboard line 107), the only trace of $4 is a thin dotted red segment over six Supply columns next to a grey '4' tick, the Demand panel has no price line at all, there is no '6 trades', no Qd=Qs, and the gold arrow lands in the middle of the MC columns. 'P=$4' and 'Qd=Qs=6' first appear as text at 4.b, after the plaza (the people) has been faded out. The on-screen definition drops the notes' first half ('price and quantity at which Qs = Qd') and keeps only 'where no one wants to change'. The convergence itself has no persistent trace (no price path, no running high/low posted price, no trade counter), and the supply-side half of the mechanism - a seller without a buyer cutting $0.25 - is a 0.3 s arrow + 0.15 s fade with no hold (in S2 the rounds jump r2->r4->r6->r9: the skipped rounds are seller cuts), while the buyer half gets two holds each time. The one frame that puts plaza + staircase + P=$4 + Qd=Qs=6 + definition together is 5.h.iii at t=546.3 of 547.3.
findings.evidence: 34_4_a.jpg (no $4 numeral, no demand-side price line, arrow tip at ~MC columns); 35_4_b.jpg (first 'P=$4', 'Qd=Qs=6', plaza gone); 65_5_h_iii.jpg (the complete synthesis frame, last teaching hold); 03_Equilibrium.py:1076-1084 (cut: FadeIn arrow + tracker 0.3 s, FadeOut 0.15 s, `continue`, no pause); 03_Equilibrium.py:1212-1221; 01_Notes.md:67 vs the on-screen string at :1213; 29_3_a_growth_S2_settled.jpg shows prices already at $4-$4.25 with only 4x4 present, i.e. the whole fall happened inside the un-narrated S2 run.
findings.why_it_matters: Signaling and temporal contiguity: a term should be attached to its referent when the referent is perceptually available. Here the word 'equilibrium' is attached to a frame in which the three defining facts (one price, equal quantities, no profitable deviation) are all invisible or unlabelled, and the verification that 'no one wants to change' is deferred ~160 s of motion and two other representations later (5.h). Transient-information effect: the causal step that actually drives price down (unsold seller undercuts) flashes for under half a second ~30 times; students cannot hold it, so the fall in price looks like something that just happens to the red dashes. This is very plausibly the 'doesn't hit the fundamentals' feeling: the fundamentals are present in the simulation but never held still and named.
findings.fix_sketch: Mostly reorder/reuse: (1) at 3.b/4.a bring in the already-built `unit_price_read` 'P=$4' and a 'Trades: 6' / 'Qd=Qs=6' readout BEFORE the definition, and draw the $4 guide across BOTH side panels; show the full notes definition. (2) Add 2-3 holds at 4.a that audit the claim on the spot using the existing 5.h close-up grammar or the existing `.declined` caption: one excluded buyer (MB $3 < $4), one excluded seller (MC $5 > $4), one trader. Consider moving 5.h.i/5.h.ii to directly after 4.a and leaving 5.h.iii as the closing recap. (3) Give seller cuts one held, captioned instance in growth ('No buyer -> cut to $5.75'), and add a persistent convergence trace: e.g. keep faint ghosts of each posted marker's previous positions on the Supply panel, or a small 'posted prices: $6.25-$4.25' range readout that rolls (style guide section 6: numbers roll).

findings.title: Salience is in the plaza; the decision-relevant information is on the side panel at ~11-15 px resolution
findings.claim: In the crowd layout the plaza disc occupies ~46% of frame width (x 432-1168 of 1600) and contains all motion; each side panel is ~19% wide. But nothing quantitative can be read in the plaza: bars are thin unscaled sticks with no dollar axis, labels and names are removed after 3.a.chosen, heights are foreshortened by depth, and matched pairs pile up along the right arc and occlude each other. The actual decision ('which seller is cheapest for me, including the +$0.25 outbid') is only on the Supply panel, where $1 = ~44 px in the extracted 1600-px frames (~59 px at native 2160), so the quarter-dollar differences that determine every choice are ~11 px (~15 px native, 1.4% of screen height), drawn red-on-red (solid 'needed' over a 0.3-opacity dashed 'posted' one tick below), with no numerals by design (storyboard line 258-260: 'one legible selected price below the graph instead of packing numerals'). The key explanatory comparison at 3.a.excluded is a teal dotted MB $6 line sitting ~11 px under a red dashed $6.25 line.
findings.evidence: 27_3_a_growth_S2_r25_b0_options.jpg (four red segments between ~$5.0 and $5.5, unlabelled; moving orb at centre); 31_3_a_growth_S7_r9_b6_options.jpg (eight columns, red ticks indistinguishable from MB $4 guide); 21_3_a_excluded.jpg and 22_3_a_excluded_reason.jpg; 19_3_a_two_pairs.jpg: caption says 'Both trades: $5.50' while the two plaza price lines sit at screen y~275 and y~387 and the two pairs' bars have different apparent lengths - equality of price is visible ONLY as one dashed line across the Supply panel; 29/30/34 frames (bar pile-up on right arc; buyer side empty; centre of screen an empty grey disc). Market_Scene_Design.md:51 already warned: 'Perspective makes distant bars look smaller, so quantitative comparisons should happen in the flat panel or in a deliberate aligned view.'
findings.why_it_matters: Lowe & Schnotz: in animations, attention follows perceptual salience (motion, size, centrality), not thematic relevance. Here salience and relevance are in different places for ~334 s. Students watching the walking orb see THAT a buyer switched, but the WHY (the price comparison) is a peripheral, low-contrast, sub-legible mark that appears for one hold. The plaza therefore teaches 'people move around' and the panel teaches nothing to a back-row student. The law of one price, the single most important visual in the episode, cannot be perceived in the 3D view at all.
findings.fix_sketch: Reuse: during any held comparison, dim the plaza (already done for non-participants at 3.a.lookout) and enlarge/centre the Supply panel, or at minimum print the 2-3 candidate prices as numerals beside the panel (small cast already does this: 15_3_a_switch_options.jpg is legible). New but modest animation: at 3.b swing the camera to the existing side-on/orthographic view (the 2.a.i and 5.h camera) with the six matched pairs lined up, so six red lines visibly sit at ONE height - 'one price' seen in the world - then return. For the crowd phase consider dropping plaza bars entirely (orbs + rings only) and letting the panels carry dollars.

findings.title: About 30 visual codes, two legends, and the red dashed/solid code reverses between plaza and panel
findings.claim: Codes a student must learn: teal/orange bars (MB/MC) and orbs (buyer/seller, never labelled as such); orb ground shadow; plaza red DASHED = contemplated offer, red SOLID = accepted (2.b gap-fill); faint red floor line = depth shadow of the price line (no economic meaning; in side view 01/06/08 it reads as a second red line joining the two people); red numeric tags per seller (exist until the third seller, then vanish); Supply-panel red LONG-DASHED = standing posted price, red SOLID = price this buyer would need (incl. +$0.25 outbid) - the reverse of the plaza convention, which the storyboard itself states (lines 81-84); dimmed dashed markers under solids; teal short-dashed MB guide drawn across a graph headed 'Supply / MC ($)'; double outline on a Demand column = the deliberating buyer; 0.45-opacity double outlines on every Supply column = options, full opacity = chosen; blue floor ring = deliberating buyer in 3.a but = 'willing buyer left out' on four waiting buyers at 5.b and on Gary at 3.a.excluded; orange floor rings on sellers = options; dashed grey hub circle = deliberation spot; grey dashed route line; docked vs undocked bars = matched vs reconsidering; 0.45 s red down-arrow = seller cut; a caption slot under the Supply panel that holds five different kinds of thing ('Posted prices', 'Price to buy', 'Buy for $5.00', '$4.25', later 'Offer to Molly: $3.25', 'Molly offers $5', 'Proposed price: $4.25'); green fill = expenditure, travelling green outline = revenue, inset orange outline = PS, teal fill = CS; on merged/aggregate graphs red fine-dashed = P/Q guide (the B1/B2 meaning students arrive with); olive/yellow thick segment = gap; dimmed people in 5.b/5.d = not participating at this price; orange boxes = produced-but-unsold unit; thick red DOTTED = proposed deviation at 5.h (a third line style). Explained on screen: 'Posted prices' and 'Price to buy' only. Red dashed therefore has at least four meanings (offer; posted price; axis guide; posted marker on the merged staircase in 5.c/5.g) plus dotted = proposal.
findings.evidence: 02_Storyboard.md:80-87 (explicit reversal), :268-275 (ring spec), :180 ('blue rings identifying the willing buyers left out'); frames 01_2_a_i.jpg, 13_3_a_overview.jpg, 15_3_a_switch_options.jpg, 24_3_a_options.jpg, 28_..._accepted.jpg ('Buy for $5.00'), 14_3_a_entry.jpg ('$4.25' in the legend slot), 46_5_b.jpg (rings on waiting buyers, dimmed sellers), 47_5_b_options.jpg, 53_5_d_i.jpg (boxes), 61_5_h_i_offer.jpg and 63_5_h_ii.jpg (dotted thick proposal over solid $4); _Style_Guide.md section 2 'every hue on screen is a noun' and section 2b RED = GUIDE 'dashed P*/Q* lines ... readouts'.
findings.why_it_matters: Each unexplained code is extraneous load that competes with the intrinsic load of the mechanism; a code whose meaning flips is worse than no code because it triggers confident misreading (a student who learned 'dashed = not yet agreed' in 2.a.i will read the dashed posted prices on the Supply panel as tentative and the solid 'price to buy' segments as done deals - exactly backwards). The style guide's own strength is that a mark means one thing everywhere; B3 is the first episode where line style, not just hue, carries state, and it does so inconsistently.
findings.fix_sketch: Decide one rule and apply it everywhere, e.g. 'solid red = a price that currently binds someone (posted or accepted); dashed red = a price someone is only considering; fine-dashed red = reading a value off an axis'. That means flipping the Supply-panel styles (posted markers solid, 'price to buy' dashed) and making the 5.h proposal dashed not dotted - a styling-only code change. Drop the floor shadow in side views (it is a depth cue with nothing to disambiguate there). Use the ring for one meaning only (deliberating); mark unserved buyers at 5.b differently or just with the gold arrow. Pin the caption slot to one job (legend) and move transient readouts elsewhere.

findings.title: Two answer sets for one question: aggregate 20 vs 45 then toy 4 vs 8 under the same title, with a third market on the exercise card
findings.claim: Representational sequence: perspective plaza (2.a) -> side-view two-bar close-up (2.a.i-2.b.vi) -> three-person close-up (2.c) -> plaza + two separated, continually rescaling unit panels (3.a) -> merged unit staircase alone (4.b) -> aggregate linear graph in thousands of pounds + algebra column (4.c-4.e) -> exercise card in galleons/pasties with Qd/Qs subscripts (4.exercise) -> aggregate graph + algebra at $3 (5.a) -> re-angled plaza beside the unit staircase with Qs=4, Qd=8 (5.b) -> aggregate at $6 (Qs=80, Qd=30) -> plaza (Qs=10, Qd=3) -> side close-up + staircase (5.h) -> plaza -> exercise card. That is ~13 switches and three unit systems. Under the single title 'What happens at $3?' students see Qs=20, Qd=45 and ~10 s of motion later Qs=4, Qd=8; under 'What happens at $6?' 80/30 then 10/3. The two markets share P*=$4 and the test prices $3/$6 by design, which invites the mapping 6 units <-> 40 thousand lb, but nothing else maps (shortage 4 vs 25; excess 7 vs 50), and the only on-screen disclaimer is the axis caption 'Q in thousands of pounds'. The notes' numbers comment even has Molly supplying 20 (thousand) at $4 in the aggregate while she is a one-unit MC-$2 seller in the plaza. The toy crossing is also not a point: MB and MC both equal $4 on units 5-6, so the staircases overlap along a plateau and 'Qd=Qs=6' depends on counting indifferent traders - a shape the linear X never has.
findings.evidence: 45_5_a.jpg (Qs=20, Qd=45) vs 46_5_b.jpg (Qs=4, Qd=8), same title; 52_5_d.jpg vs 53_5_d_i.jpg; 35_4_b.jpg (plateau overlap at $4 between Q=4 and 6); 36_4_c.jpg; 42_4_exercise.jpg; 02_Storyboard.md:157 ('These curves represent a larger market, not a rescaling of six people'), :190-192 ('The two representations share price, not quantity'), :145-150; 01_Notes.md:6.
findings.why_it_matters: Split attention across time plus an unresolved identity question ('is the line graph the same market zoomed out?') forces students to hold two number sets and decide which one 'the answer' is, exactly when the new terms shortage/excess are being attached. The students' exercise (Q2) is purely the algebraic version, so the toy numbers are the ones most likely to be discarded - yet the toy plaza is where the incentive story (the thing skill B3.1 bullet 4 asks for) lives. The engineered coincidence of $4 makes the two look like one market while the quantities say they are not, which is the worst of both worlds.
findings.fix_sketch: Reorder of existing assets: for each deviation go plaza-first (5.b: see the queue, name it, watch the price climb) and only then 'now the same question with equations' (5.a algebra) as the bridge into Exercise Q2 - one number set on screen per title. Add one explicit bridging hold at 4.c where the staircase visibly smooths/relabels into the line graph with a caption such as 'Many more buyers and sellers: steps become lines' so the relation is stated rather than implied. Longer-term: either make the aggregate a true scale-up of the toy (choose D/S lines that pass through the toy staircase so 6 units <-> 6 thousand) or deliberately give it a different P* so nobody maps them.

findings.title: Pause questions elicit one-step individual yes/no judgments; no hold asks for a market-level prediction that students could actually make
findings.claim: Bottom gold prompts, in order: 'Would they both accept this price?'; 'Would Amanda-Grace gain by offering $4.25?'; 'Would Amanda-Grace keep paying $6.25?'; 'Could Gary gain by offering $4.50?'; 'Would Molly lower her price?'; 'Would the new buyer offer $5.75?'; 'Why is Gary left out?'; 'Would Gary trade with the new seller?'; then none for 104 growth stops; 'Would Amanda-Grace offer Molly $3.25?'; 'Would Gary switch from Andrew to Molly?'; 'Would these sellers produce at $4?'; 'Would this buyer accept?'; 'Would this seller accept?'. All but one are yes/no, about one named individual, answerable by a single visible comparison, and the answer is 'yes' every time until 5.g.production/5.h where it is 'no'. The only why-question is 'Why is Gary left out?' (the best prompt in the episode). Market-level questions exist only as azure titles - 'Where do prices settle?', 'What happens at $3?', 'Would anyone gain by changing?' - and the first is unanswerable when posed: at 3.a.plaza there are two buyers and one seller on screen, the side panels do not exist yet, and their x-axes grow from 0-2 to 0-10 with a different unit width on each side, so the full MB/MC schedules a student would need in order to predict $4 or 'six trades' are not visible until 3.b, when the answer is already there. 'What happens at $3?' is immediately answered by algebra rather than held as a prediction over the settled plaza. No prompt asks 'what happens to the price when a third buyer arrives and there are only two units?', 'who gets left out?', 'how many trades?', or 'which way does price move?' before the motion shows it.
findings.evidence: 03_Equilibrium.py:151, :385, :816, :882, :950, :1010, :1873, :1956 (all prompt strings); 12_3_a_plaza.jpg (title posed with 3 people, no graphs); 13/20/26/30/31/34 frames (x-axis labels 0-2, 0-3, 0-4, 0-7/0-6, 0-8, 0-10); 02_Storyboard.md:223-226; 43_5_a_s_question.jpg -> 44_5_a_s_algebra.jpg sequence in INDEX.txt (question -> algebra within 3.7 s of motion).
findings.why_it_matters: Generative processing comes from committing to a prediction and then seeing it confirmed or violated. Yes/no prompts with visible answers produce recognition, not inference, and repeated 'yes' answers train students to stop thinking by the third one. The intellectual content of B3 is that individually trivial decisions aggregate into a non-obvious market outcome; if every elicited thought is at the trivial level, the non-obvious level is only ever told, never reasoned. It also starves Taylor's improvisation: a 'would X do Y?' hold supports ten seconds of talk, a 'where will this end up and why?' hold supports three minutes.
findings.fix_sketch: Pre-training + prediction, mostly reuse: before growth (after 3.a.chosen) flash the full ten-MB and ten-MC sorted panels on fixed 0-10 axes (they already exist at 3.b) with the question 'Ten buyers, ten sellers. What price? How many trades?' - hold, take guesses - then fade back and run the compressed growth to confirm. Keep panel axes fixed at 0-10 throughout so columns do not resize/re-rank on every arrival. Convert three existing holds to market-level predictions by caption change only: 3.a.third_buyer 'Three buyers, two units: what happens to the price? Who goes home empty-handed?'; 5.b 'Four units, eight willing buyers: what does a left-out buyer do?'; 5.d.i 'Seven unsold units: what does a seller with no buyer do?'. Hold 'What happens at $3?' over the settled plaza before any algebra.

findings.title: What 3D buys and what it costs
findings.claim: 3D carries meaning in exactly three places: (a) the continuous pullback 2.c.iii -> 3.a.plaza, which preserves identity from a two-bar exchange to dots in a market (micro-to-macro continuity, the episode's real 3D payoff); (b) walking between floor stations = switching trading partner, with the hub as 'thinking' and the arcs as buyer/seller sides (floor position = role; this is planar information, a top-down 2D view would carry it equally); (c) nontraders physically remaining on their arcs at 4.a/5.h.iii. Height-as-dollars, the feature that nominally justifies the third dimension, is not readable in the perspective view (no axis, foreshortening, thin sticks, occlusion) and every quantitative read is therefore duplicated on flat panels - a permanent split-attention tax that exists only because of 3D. Every frame in which the episode is clearest is one where 3D has been turned off: the orthographic side views 2.a.i-2.c.iii and 5.h.i/5.h.ii (shared baseline, big labels on the bars, one question). 3D also generates its own codes and defects: floor shadows for price lines, camera-facing text logic, the re-angled plaza in section 5 (disc now left and tilted differently from 3.a), label collisions and clipping ('New buye' cut by a bar at 3.a.excluded; 'Amanda Grace'/'Molly' overlapping at 3.a.entry; gold arrow through 'Amanda-Grace' at 5.b), and the right-arc bar pile-up once pairs dock at the seller.
findings.evidence: 00_2_a.jpg (perspective, bars unscaled) vs 01_2_a_i.jpg/06_2_b_vi.jpg/08_2_c_i.jpg/11_2_c_iii.jpg (side view, fully legible); 12_3_a_plaza.jpg (pullback result); 14_3_a_entry.jpg, 21_3_a_excluded.jpg, 46_5_b.jpg (collisions); 34_4_a.jpg, 51_5_c.jpg, 58_5_g_production.jpg (pile-up); 61/63 (close-ups); 02_Storyboard.md:36-46 (world-text machinery), :48-53 (stroke/shadow tuning needed only for 3D legibility).
findings.why_it_matters: Tversky's congruence principle: animation helps when the motion's structure matches the concept's structure. Walking-to-a-seller is congruent with 'choosing a seller'; zooming out is congruent with 'one exchange among many'. Bar height in perspective is NOT congruent with 'dollar amount' because the mapping from screen length to dollars changes with depth, so the representation silently violates the one-dollar-scale invariant the design doc asked for. The cost is paid for ~60% of the episode; the benefit is concentrated in perhaps three transitions.
findings.fix_sketch: Keep 3D for the pullback, the walking, and the nontraders tableau. At crowd scale either remove plaza bars (orbs + rings; dollars live only on panels) or switch the crowd camera to a low-elevation orthographic projection with sellers on a line of constant depth so equal prices land at equal screen heights. Use the side-on camera (already built for 2.a.i and 5.h) for every moment where a dollar comparison is the point. Keep the section-5 plaza at the same camera pose and screen position as 3.a so the scene is recognisably the same place.

findings.title: Rescaling, re-ranking side panels and a hybrid 'Supply' graph
findings.claim: From 3.a.overview to 3.b both panels keep a fixed physical width while their x-range grows with the head-count, so bar widths shrink at each arrival, the two panels frequently have different unit widths in the same frame (Demand 0-3 beside Supply 0-2; Demand 0-7 beside Supply 0-6), and because newcomers are inserted in sorted order an existing person's column changes rank and position (Gary's MB-$6 column is 2nd of 2, then 3rd of 3, 3rd of 4, ...). Meanwhile the right panel, headed 'Supply / MC ($)', carries four layers at once during a decision: MC columns, dashed posted prices floating above them, solid 'price to buy' segments, and a teal demand-side MB line with its own label - so the graph students were taught in B2 to read as 'the supply curve' temporarily has a demand object and two price layers on it, then at 4.b the price layers vanish and the MC tops are 'supply' again.
findings.evidence: 13_3_a_overview.jpg (0-2 | 0-1), 20_3_a_third_options.jpg (0-3 | 0-2), 30_3_a_growth_B6_declined.jpg (0-7 | 0-6), 31_..._S7_...jpg (0-8 | 0-8), 34_4_a.jpg (0-10 | 0-10); 02_Storyboard.md:223-227, :256-262; 15_3_a_switch_options.jpg and 24_3_a_options.jpg (MB label and red prices on the Supply panel).
findings.why_it_matters: Pre-training principle: students should have a stable schema for the graph before it is used to explain something. A panel whose scale, column identities and layer set change every few holds cannot become a stable referent, so each decision requires re-parsing the panel (extraneous load) rather than reading it. Posted prices hovering above MC is economically right and pedagogically valuable (price is not cost), but it is never said on screen and competes with the B2 identity 'supply curve = MC'.
findings.fix_sketch: Fix both panels at 0-10 from 3.a.overview with empty slots (ghost outlines) that fill as people arrive, in arrival order until 3.b, then do one explicit 'sort' play before the merge (this also restores the 'where curves come from' beat from Market_Scene_Design.md step 3). Add one early hold whose only job is to read the Supply panel: 'orange = what it costs her; red = what she is asking'.

findings.title: Accounting block front-loads five B1/B2 terms that B3 never uses again
findings.claim: 2.b.i-2.b.vi spend 6 stops (2.7%) and introduce Expenditure, CS, Revenue, MC-as-area, PS plus a new colour event (green outline travels and becomes Revenue; orange inset outline = PS) before the episode's own question has been posed. None of these areas reappears after 2.b.vi, none is assessed in Exercise B3 or skill B3.1; they belong to B4. The block gets three times the holds of definition+merge.
findings.evidence: 06_2_b_vi.jpg (seven labels on one frame: MB, CS, Price, Expenditure, Revenue, PS, MC, plus 'One unit'); 02_Storyboard.md:62-68; B_Skillsheet.typ:107-116; Exercise_B3.typ.
findings.why_it_matters: Coherence principle: material that is interesting and correct but not needed for the current learning goal consumes capacity at the start of the lesson, when students are forming their sense of 'what today is about'. The one idea B3 needs from this block - any price between MC and MB works, and the price splits the gain - is carried by 2.a.i + 2.b alone.
findings.fix_sketch: Reorder/skip only: in B3 stop at 2.b plus a single hold showing the two gains (CS $2, PS $2) and go to 2.c; keep the full 2.b.i-2.b.vi build for the opening of B4, where total surplus is the topic. No new animation.

findings.title: An assessed skill is visible but unsignaled: quantity exchanged = the short side
findings.claim: Skill B3.1 bullet 3 asks students to find quantity exchanged as the smaller of Qd and Qs. The plaza shows it perfectly - four docked pairs at $3, three at $6 - but no readout, caption or hold names it; the frames show only Qs and Qd.
findings.evidence: B_Skillsheet.typ:115; 46_5_b.jpg (Qs=4, Qd=8, four matched pairs, no 'exchanged' readout); 53_5_d_i.jpg (Qd=3, Qs=10).
findings.why_it_matters: The 3D world is doing real work here (you can count the pairs) and the opportunity to convert it into an assessed skill is one label away.
findings.fix_sketch: Script-level: add a red 'Exchanged: 4' (then '3') readout at 5.b and 5.d.i, ideally with a brief highlight of the docked pairs; one extra hold each.

what_works: The orthographic side-view close-ups (2.a.i through 2.c.iii, and 5.h.i/5.h.ii): shared baseline, bars as large labelled rectangles, price line spanning exactly the two bars, one gold question. These are the most legible frames in the episode and have excellent spatial contiguity (labels on the objects).

2.b.iii: the green expenditure boundary physically sliding from Gary's bar to Molly's and being relabelled Revenue - motion that is congruent with the idea (the same $4 seen from two sides). Preserve for B4 even if trimmed from B3.

2.c.ii -> 2.c.iii: seven quarter-dollar bids compressed into one 14 s play ending on 'Gary: next bid $6.50 > MB $6'. This is the right worked-example-then-compress rhythm and is the template the growth phase should copy.

3.a.excluded / 3.a.excluded.reason: 'Why is Gary left out?' then 'Gary traded at $5.50. Now $6.25 > MB $6.' Same person, same MB, different outcome because of who else arrived - the one genuinely market-level why-question, and it lands on a stable frame.

5.b and 5.d.i: definition at the bottom, gold arrow to the actual phenomenon in the world (ringed waiting buyers; orange unsold-unit boxes), and Qs/Qd drops on the adjacent staircase - term, referent and numbers in one frame. The unsold-unit box is an economical, countable glyph.
5.g.production ('Would these sellers produce at $4?') - the only place the quantity side of adjustment is made explicit, and it uses the boxes well.
5.h.iii: plaza with nontraders still present + staircase + P=$4 + Qd=Qs=6 + definition. This is the frame the lesson is about; it should appear much earlier as well as here.

The algebra staging (4.c.i-4.e, 5.a, 5.d): curve-coloured terms carried from graph labels into the working, P*=? / Q*=? shown before the answer, results carried back to the axes. It mirrors Exercise Q1/Q2 step for step and is the best-aligned part of the episode to what is assessed.
4.b builds the staircases from the very columns students have watched accumulate, and keeps equal-height units as plateaus - object continuity across a representation change.

Teacher-paced holds as the segmenting mechanism is the right architecture; the problem is allocation of holds, not the mechanism. The one-dollar z-scale and the model/visual assertions mean what is on screen is always true to the simulation.
open_questions: How did Taylor actually traverse the 110 growth stops in class - individually, by holding advance, or by jumping to 3.b? The diagnosis of 'over-segmented' vs 'long un-narrated transient' depends on this, though both are problems.

Was the 1.a/1.b recap (twin B1/B2 graphs, the 'floating price' question) delivered verbally only? The export goes 0.a -> 2.a, so the motivating market-level question has no visual and the first on-screen question is about two people.
Room/projector: at native 2160 px a $0.25 step on the side panels is ~15 px (1.4% of screen height). Is that resolvable from the back row?

Is the toy fixture's plateau at $4 (MB = MC = $4 on units 5-6, so the staircases overlap and Qd=Qs=6 relies on indifferent traders) intended? A fixture with a clean crossing would make 4.b look like the X students will draw.
Do students have the exercise sheet in hand during the animation? If so the pasties market is a third concurrent representation during 4.c-5.a.

Is sharing P*=$4 and the $3/$6 test prices between the toy and the aggregate market a deliberate bridge Taylor wants to keep? If yes, the bridge needs to be stated on screen; if not, the aggregate should either be a true scale-up of the toy or clearly different.
Did the dashed/solid reversal actually confuse anyone, or did students simply not attend to line style at all (which would itself indicate the panels were not being read)?

verdicts.title: Budget inversion: half the holds are one repeated micro-decision; the thesis gets two holds
verdicts.note: Recomputed from present.json (225 stops, 224 named, 547.3 s). Numbers hold to within 1-3 stops: 3.a.* = 127 stops / 334.0 s (61% of motion); small cast 3.a.plaza..3.a.chosen = 18 stops / 98.9 s; growth = 107 named growth stops + 3.a.i + 3.a.ii (109, reviewer says 110) / 235.1 s; S2 arrival = 47 stops / 119.4 s = 21.8% of all motion, 23 options->accepted pairs + settled; B2 = 20 / 42.7 s; other 12 arrivals = 40 stops / 73.0 s with 6 '.declined'; 4.a = 1 stop / 1.0 s; 4.b = 1 / 4.3 s. Suffix counts exact: 49 .options, 40 .accepted, 6 .declined, 42 .roundN = 137/224 (61%). index.html:284-292 confirms every stop costs one keypress (playToNextStop); the only bypass is clicking a rail chip, and the whole of 3.a.entry..S9.settled is ONE unit (unit 45, 124 stops), so there is no clean 'skip to next arrival'. Code :1129 and :1183 confirmed as the per-decision pauses; Market_Scene_Design.md:60 quote ('Demonstrate one decision slowly, then compress the remaining visits') and notes 3.a/3.b ('continuous action', 'calmer and calmer') confirmed verbatim; 2.c.ii->2.c.iii is one 13.9 s play. Overstatements: (1) 'the same two frame templates' is wrong for the 42 .roundN stops - those are 5.c/5.g frames (57_5_g_round15.jpg): no hub, no MB guide, no caption at all; a third, wordless template.
