findings.claim: B1 and B2 built a single tool: a red price line on a (Q,P) graph, traced across to the curve and down to a red Q_d or Q_s. B3's discovery section never uses it. The side panels are MB/MC bar charts over 'Units'. The demand panel never gets a price line, only a highlighted column. The supply panel carries four overlaid things: MC bars, dashed red posted prices per seller, solid red 'Price to buy' ticks per seller that include the $0.25 outbid increment, and a dotted teal MB guide. Qd and Qs first appear at 4.b (t=390.8s) as a finished answer, 'Qd=Qs=6'. They are first computed at a price in 5.a (t=416–430s). Roughly 18 of 224 stops show one market price with Qd/Qs readouts.
findings.evidence: Frames 15_3_a_switch_options.jpg, 24_3_a_options.jpg, 27_3_a_growth_S2_r25_b0_options.jpg ('Price to buy', teal 'MB $6' dashed line over the Supply panel, 3–4 separate red ticks). Storyboard 02_Storyboard.md:80–87 and :256–266. 03_Equilibrium.py:700, :988, :1108 ('Price to buy'); first Q_d text at :1273. `grep ValueTracker 03_Equilibrium.py` finds only per-seller ask and pairing trackers (:491, :494), no market-price tracker; B1 and B2 contain tracker code throughout (grep counts 36 and 28 of tracker/set_value lines). Contrast Style Guide §4 'Reading a graph and doing the math' steps 1–5 and 'Selected-quantity readouts use Q_d ... Q_s'. B2 storyboard 3.m binds world (farm) and graph to one price tracker.
findings.why_it_matters: By week 4 the students' trained move is 'find the red line, read across, read down'. For six minutes of motion the screen offers up to ten red marks and no 'the price'. Students cannot apply what B1/B2 gave them and have to learn a new outbid/posted-ask mechanism that is never assessed. When Qd=Qs finally appears, nothing they watched produced it.
findings.fix_sketch: Small new animation on existing assets. At the four small-market settle holds, draw one red horizontal price line across both side panels with red Q_d and Q_s readouts under each. This is B2's 8.a device and reuses 4.b's guide code. The holds are 3.a.two_pairs ($5.50: Qd 2, Qs 2); 3.a.third_buyer ($5.50: Qd 3, Qs 2, which makes 'Three buyers. Two units.' a B1/B2 read); 3.a.excluded ($6.25: Qd 2, Qs 2, which answers 'Why is Gary left out?' off the demand panel); and 3.b/4.a ($4: 6 and 6). Keep the bilateral deliberation for the named cast only.

findings.title: The 4.a definition card names something students did not watch and drops the assessed half
findings.claim: The on-screen definition at 4.a is 'Equilibrium is where no one wants to change.' The notes' definition is 'The price and quantity at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded — where no one wants to change.' Skillsheet B3.1 says 'At equilibrium, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied'. B5's callback assumes both halves fused: 'only one price where neither buyer nor seller would want to change their price: Q_S = Q_D'. At 4.a the screen has no Qd, no Qs, and no price line across demand. A gold arrow points at a short dotted $4 segment on the Supply panel. 'No one wants to change' is asserted there and only tested at 5.h, 145 seconds of motion and an exercise later. The equivalence between no-one-wants-to-change and Qd=Qs gets one static frame (4.b), and that crossing is a two-unit plateau overlap rather than a point.
findings.evidence: Frame 34_4_a.jpg; 03_Equilibrium.py:1212–1221, with the same card text reused at :2008. 01_Notes.md:67 versus B_Skillsheet.typ:109–113; B5_Changes/01_Notes.md:92. Frame 35_4_b.jpg shows D and S overlapping on units 4–6 at $4. Storyboard :145–150: 'Qd = Qs = 6, counting indifferent participants'.
findings.why_it_matters: Taylor's christening pattern (Style Guide §9 'Abstractions are earned: one concrete instance first'; §3 'Term appears in the script first ... the card comes after') works because the gold word lands on the object just watched. Here the object watched is 'individual renegotiations stopped'. The object assessed, and needed by B4/B5, is 'the price where Qd=Qs'. The bridge between them is what the episode exists to teach, and it goes by without a hold.
findings.fix_sketch: Script plus one-line code change. Put the notes' full definition on the card (:1213, :2008). Before the card, at 3.b, show the common $4 line across both side panels with Qd=6 and Qs=6 (same asset as the previous finding). Then make the 4.a hold carry the notes' four-way 'would anyone change?' argument. Optionally use a fixture whose curves cross at a point, for example MC of 3.5 and 4.5 in place of the two 4s, so the first crossing is clean and B4's 'efficient quantity' is not 4-or-6.

findings.title: B3 is a structural outlier against Taylor's own B1/B2 pattern
findings.claim: B2's export has 176s of motion and 84 stops, with the first gold definition at 2.b, t=22s (12%). B1 has 179s, with the first definition at its second elicitation beat (B05b). Both live on the (Q,P) plane from the first content beat, and Exercise Q1 lands mid-episode (B2 3.n at 75s, 43%). B3 has 547s and 224 named stops, with the first definition at 386.5s (71%), the first combined (Q,P) graph at 390.8s, and Exercise Q1 at 411s (75%). One seller's arrival (3.a.growth.S2) takes 47 stops and 119s, two-thirds of all of B2. Arrivals/growth take 128 stops and 61% of motion. The algebra (4.c–4.e) is 7 stops and 3.5%. findings.why_it_matters: With improvised talk, holds set the lesson's rhythm. B1/B2 loop from concrete instance to name to price move to algebra about every 10–20s of motion. B3 asks students to hold an unnamed phenomenon across 142 stops, and the assessed material (algebra, Qd/Qs at a price, direction) ends up in the last quarter when attention and class time are lowest. findings.title: One-at-a-time arrivals are B5 comparative statics performed 17 times before equilibrium is defined
findings.claim: Each arrival adds a bar, re-sorts the panel, and rescales its x-axis (0–2, 0–3, ..., 0–10, with bar widths shrinking). That is B5.1's 'number of buyers/sellers' shifter. Each arrival is followed by a re-settle to a new price, which is B5.3. Under the persistent title 'Where do prices settle?', students see the answers $5.50 (3.a.two_pairs), $6.25 (3.a.excluded), a mix after the third seller, and finally $4. Each of those is a genuine equilibrium of a different market. The population keeps changing, so students never see a fixed market converge to its one price, and the final $4 reads as wherever the last arrival left things.
findings.evidence: Storyboard :99–113 and :220–227 ('Their horizontal scale expands from the current participant count to ten; bar widths shrink as people join'). Frames 19 (axis 0–2), 21 (0–3 / 0–2), 27 (0–4), 34 (0–10). B5_Changes/01_Notes.md:37: 'every time another seller opens their doors the supply curve shifts out'. B_Skillsheet.typ:146–148, :167. Storyboard :204–205 records sequential arrivals as Taylor's own review request.
findings.why_it_matters: B3's fundamental is that a given pair of curves has one price where Qd=Qs and the market is pushed to it. Moving the curves 17 times before that is established gives 'settle' several numerical answers in one episode. It also spends B5's central demonstration in unnamed form, and B5 will have to rebuild it.
findings.fix_sketch: Reorder existing assets. Keep arrivals only while building the named cast: second buyer means price up, second seller means price down. Those two are unlabeled shortage and excess and are useful. Then fade in all ten-by-ten at once with curves fixed and let that fixed market converge. Save 'a new buyer walks in' for B5, where the same plaza can replay it as a named shift.

findings.title: The shot B2 promised and B4/B5 need is missing: one price tracker sweeping the combined graph with Qd/Qs attached

The shown animation has no 1.a/1.b; it goes 0.a to 2.a 'Would they exchange?'. B4's notes ask for that device ('*~Start with price far from equilibrium, and let it oscillate toward equilibrium.*'), and B5's shortage-then-price-rises-to-new-equilibrium step depends on it.
findings.evidence: B2_Supply/02_Storyboard.md:142–143 (8.a). _Style_Guide.md:337–341. 01_Notes.md:13–23 (1.a, 1.b) versus the stop list (0.a@7.3s then 2.a@11.3s; no `1.` pauses in 03_Equilibrium.py). Second, a small new animation on the 5.a aggregate graph: after the gap highlight, roll one price ValueTracker from $3 to $4 with both dots, drops, Q_s and Q_d readouts attached and the gap line shrinking to zero, then repeat from $6 to $4. Collapse the 5.c and 5.g rounds to one continuous run each, keeping the common price line visible.

findings.title: Assessed B3.1 skills get a small, late share of the holds; two sub-skills get none
findings.claim: Against the four B3.1 standard bullets: (1) Plot S&D and solve by setting Qd=Qs gets 4.c through 4.exercise, about 9 stops (4%) and about 25s (4.5%). (2) Qd and Qs at a price, shortage/excess, and measuring its size get 5.a.*, 5.b, 5.d.*, 5.d.i, 5.e, 5.exercise, about 14 stops (6%) and about 46s (8%); the gap is highlighted but never given a number (no '25' or '50' anywhere), although Exercise Q2c asks 'how large?'. findings.title: The simulation drifted from companion sidecar to main episode, against the original concept's own guardrails
findings.claim: Before the restage the episode was a B1/B2-scale graph lesson (shortage, excess, 'can a price not change?', equilibrium, algebra, stable), and the 3D market was 'a companion video'. The restage merged the companion in and put it first, and the 09-21 passes expanded it. Several guardrails from the original sources were dropped along the way. Bx_Equilibrium_Video.typ says 'keep referencing the standard market graph as it goes'; the notes now say 'kept apart; no combined graph or crossing until 4.e'. Market_Scene_Design.md says 'Demonstrate one decision slowly, then compress the remaining visits', yet every growth decision now has `.lookout/.options/.accepted` stops. The design doc says the competitive benchmark with 'a supporting uniform price' is the mode 'useful for teaching demand, supply, welfare', that the decentralized process should come after those representations work ('Add decentralized repricing after...'), that one should 'Show intended demand, intended supply, and completed trades as different quantities', and that 'quantitative comparisons should happen in the flat panel'. The decentralized process is now the main event, and intended demand/supply are not shown until 5.b. The original 'as we break decisions into smaller and smaller parts, this looks more and more like a line' became a hard cut at 4.c, where the six-unit toy and the 40-thousand-pound algebra market share only the number $4, although notes 4.e claims the star lands 'exactly where the market settled'.
findings.evidence: _archive/01_Notes_pre_restage_2026-09-20.md:19 ('In a companion video'), :149–189. Bx_Market_Animation/Bx_Equilibrium_Video.typ:100, :98. Market_Scene_Design.md:51, :60, :63, :83–87, :143–145. Storyboard :16–18 ('old episode/companion division ... do not govern this new single episode'), :157 ('not a rescaling of six people'), :190–192 ('share price, not quantity'). Faithful to the original: the sorted-MC price search ('do it with an ordered MC to show it's not a mystery'), nontraders kept visible, and the 'someone tries to switch' test at 5.h.
findings.why_it_matters: The original design kept the world as an illustration of the standard graph, with one slow decision, the rest compressed, and a uniform price visible. The implementation reversed that: the graph became a late annotation of the world. That reversal produces the feeling of the right goal with something slightly off.
findings.fix_sketch: Structural reorder, no new assets. Treat 2.a–3.a.chosen (about 150s) as the in-episode discovery and move the full one-by-one growth back to a companion or recitation video. For the toy-to-line bridge, reuse B1's idiom ('many thin bars' under the line, B1 storyboard B17) on the 4.c axes so the staircase visibly becomes the line instead of being replaced.

findings.title: 2.a/2.b recalls B1/B2 vocabulary faithfully but points at B4's question and skips the price experiment that poses B3's question
findings.claim: The 2.b close-up (Expenditure $4, CS $2, Revenue $4, MC $2, PS $2; 7 stops, about 11s) uses B1/B2 tokens and reveal order correctly. But surplus never returns in B3: 2.c already says 'gains $7−$4.25', not CS, so the five labels have no later job. A week ahead, they frame the opening as 'how good is this trade?', which is B4's question. The B1/B2 idiom that would have posed B3's question is absent. Every B1/B2 single-bar close-up runs a price experiment (B1 B12c raises the price above the bar and lowers it; B2 has 4.d.1.price-low, no-sale, price-high). Here the price sits at $4 and is accepted, so the notes' key line, 'any price between $2 and $6 would have worked — the same window we saw in Part A', has no picture. The arbitrary first offer ($4) also equals the eventual toy equilibrium ($4) and the algebra P* ($4).
findings.evidence: Frames 01_2_a_i.jpg, 05_2_b_v.jpg. 01_Notes.md:33, :39. B1 storyboard B12c/B12c2. B2 storyboard 4.b.1–4.d.10. Pre-restage ED note (:153): 'the .typ overlays CS/PS during the sim — under the new ladder those belong to B4, so the companion should soft-pedal them', later overridden by Taylor's 09-20 direction. Style Guide §9: 'a mark with no job in the current beat is clutter'. B4 notes ED (:5) already flags that CS/PS 'now read as re-builds'.
findings.why_it_matters: The pair's role in B3 is to show that two people alone leave the price undetermined (a $2–$6 window), and competition then pins it down. Without the window, 'where do prices come from?' is not yet a puzzle when the bidding war starts. With the first offer at $4, students can reasonably think $4 was given from the start.
findings.fix_sketch: Small new animation using 2.c's existing rolling-price choreography. At 2.a.i roll the dashed offer to $7 (Gary's bar greys, as in B1 B12c), then $1.50 (Molly's greys, as in B2 'no-sale'), then bracket $2–$6 with the hold 'Any price here works. Which one?'. Start the first deal at $3 or $5, not $4. Shrink 2.b to two holds (buyer side, seller side), or move it to the B4 opener where it has a job.

findings.title: The stability tests (5.h) justify 'no one wants to change' with marginal-unit logic that generalizes wrongly
findings.claim: 5.h.i shows the MB-$4 buyer refusing $4.25 with the on-screen reason '$4.25 > MB $4', and 5.h.ii shows the MC-$4 seller refusing $3.75 because '$3.75 < MC $4'. That reason holds only for the zero-surplus tie participants. The MB-$8 buyer would also refuse $4.25, but because other sellers offer $4, not because of MB. The notes' four-case argument ('If a seller raised their price, they would lose all their business ...') is the competitive logic, and it is what ties 'no one wants to change' to Qd=Qs: there is no left-out buyer to bid against and no unsold unit to undercut.
findings.evidence: Frame 62_5_h_i.jpg. 03_Equilibrium.py:1949–1995. Storyboard :187 ('Test actual marginal participants'). 01_Notes.md:63–65, :163–165.
findings.why_it_matters: Students can leave believing that equilibrium holds because MB equals price for buyers. That is false for five of the six traders and conflicts with B4, where inframarginal surplus is the main point.
findings.fix_sketch: Script plus choice of participant. Test an inframarginal pair, for example the MB-$8 buyer's seller asks $4.25, and show the buyer's MB guide across the supply staircase with other $4 asks available (the existing `.options` survey asset), so the refusal reads as 'someone else sells at $4'. Keep one marginal test as the second case.

findings.title: Visual-vocabulary drift from the B1/B2 graph conventions
findings.claim: Red was 'One accent, always red', meaning the price and the selected quantity. In the plaza it marks up to six accepted-price lines, up to ten dashed posted prices, solid 'Price to buy' ticks, and floating numbers at once. None of the side panels, the 4.b unit graph, or the 4.c aggregate graph carries the white 'P' and 'Q' axis names that §4 makes invariant; they say 'MB ($)'/'Units', 'Dollars per unit', and 'Q in thousands of pounds'. The shortage gap uses the DEFINITION gold text token on geometry. The persistent title 'Where do prices settle?' covers 54s to 386s.
findings.evidence: _Style_Guide.md §2b GUIDE row, §4 axis-label bullet, and §2 'DEFINITION gold belongs to terms, not curves'. Frames 27, 34, 35, 41. 03_Equilibrium.py:1555–1556.
findings.why_it_matters: Each item is small. Together they mean the B3 graphs do not look like the B1/B2 graphs students practiced on, so the recognition the style guide is built to produce does not fire during the long section.
findings.fix_sketch: Code-only tidy. Add white P/Q axis names to the side panels and both combined graphs. Switch the gap line to FOCUS. When the price-line read from the first finding is on screen, dim per-seller ticks to MUTED so one red line dominates.

what_works: 5.a and 5.d (frames 45_5_a.jpg, 52) are model B1/B2 beats: red P input, colored equation copies carried into the math area, Q_s=? and Q_d=? withheld until solved, answers carried back to the axis, grey divider. This is the engine doing its job. Preserve it and move it earlier.

5.b and 5.d.i (frames 46, 53) are the best frames in the episode: plaza and unit graph side by side at one price, Qs=4/Qd=8 with ringed left-out buyers, Qd=3/Qs=10 with orange unsold-unit boxes, and the gold definition with an arrow to the phenomenon. They are the christening pattern done right, and B4's ceiling/floor can reuse them directly.

The 4.c–4.e algebra (frame 41) follows §4/§6 exactly: curve-colored terms keep their color until combined, red Q and P, Q*=? and P*=? unknown until solved, 40 travels into the substitution, stars on the graph.

The small-market beats are strong phenomenon-first material that B5 and B4 can call back to: 2.c (a second buyer bids the price up to $6.25, stopping at 'Gary: next bid $6.50 > MB $6'); 3.a.seller.cut ('Would Molly lower her price?'); 3.a.excluded/.reason ('Gary traded at $5.50. Now $6.25 > MB $6'). They are unlabeled shortage, excess, and rationing-by-value with a named cast. They need a Qd/Qs read, not removal.
The continuing cast and numbers are coherent with B1/B2: Gary, Amanda-Grace, Molly, Andrew; B1's D: P=12−Q/5 rides through; pounds; and the pasty curve P=12−Q/2 is reused in the exercises.
'Excess, not surplus' at 5.e and Amanda-Grace's $3.25 line-jump at 5.b.i are exactly what B4's notes call back to (B4 notes :165 and :267–281). Keep both.
The exercise cards (4.exercise, 5.exercise) match Exercise_B3.typ verbatim, land after the concept is named as _Parts.md requires, and give no answers.

The sorted-MC survey (a buyer's MB guide across the ordered supply columns) is faithful to the original concept's 'do it with an ordered MC to show it's not a mystery'. It is a good one-time explanation of how a buyer finds the best price. It should be shown once or twice, not 49 times.

The pure-rules separation (Sim/discovery.py with tests; the storyboard's honest caveat that the demonstrated path is 'not a proof of general convergence') follows Market_Scene_Design's requirement that outcomes come from model state, not scripted motion.
open_questions: How much class time did 2.a–3.b consume? If the pre-definition section took more than about half the period, the pacing diagnosis is confirmed. If Taylor skipped through the growth stops quickly, the problem is more about apparatus than duration.
Were both exercises reached and completed in class, and how did Q2c ('how large?') and the direction question go? That directly tests whether the late 5.a–5.g material landed.
Did Taylor verbally recap B1/B2 (notes 1.a/1.b) with nothing on screen? Opening on B2's literal 8.a frame would be a cheap way to tell whether the missing handoff mattered.

Is the one-at-a-time growth to 10×10 something Taylor wants students to watch, or was it requested (storyboard :204) to fix simultaneous entrances looking chaotic? If the latter, a fixed 10×10 continuous settle serves the fundamentals better and leaves arrivals for B5.

Should 'quantity exchanged = the smaller of Qd and Qs' (B3.1 bullet 3) be taught in B3 at all, or formally moved to B4.2 where the notes' Q&A already covers it? At present no animation or exercise in B3 covers it, yet the B3 skill standard lists it.

Is the $4 = $4 coincidence between the toy and the algebra market meant as the bridge (notes 4.e: 'exactly where the market settled')? If so, the quantity mismatch (6 units versus 40 thousand lb) needs a spoken or visual reconciliation. If not, distinct numbers would reduce false linkage.

The restage moved shortage/excess from before the definition to after it, as 'tests'. Does Taylor want them to keep their original motivating role? A hybrid is possible: small-market discovery, then shortage at $3 and excess at $6 on the combined graph as the argument for equilibrium, then the definition, algebra, stability, and exercises.

verdicts.title: The B1/B2 engine (one price, read a quantity) is missing from the first 386 seconds
verdicts.note: Verified: there is no market-price tracker in 03_Equilibrium.py. ValueTracker is created only at :491 and :494 (per-bar pairing and per-seller ask). 'Price to buy' appears at :700, :988 and :1108. The first Q_d/Q_s text is at :1273 (4.b, t=390.8s). Frame 27 shows four solid red ticks, faint dashed posted marks and a teal MB $6 guide over the Supply panel, and nothing red on the Demand panel. The style guide's five reading steps (:246-263) are real. My tracker/set_value grep counts came out 52 (B1), 42 (B2) and 53 (B3), which differ from the reviewer's 36 and 28, but this does not change the point. Overstated: 'no single market price exists' and 'ten red marks and no the price'. At the named small-market settles the per-seller dashes coincide into one red dashed line across the whole Supply panel, with plaza price labels (frame 19: $5.50; frame 21: $6.25). Frame 21 already draws Gary's teal MB $6 guide directly under the red $6.25 line, which is a price-versus-MB read. Frame 34 (4.a) has one dotted $4 line over supply units 0-6. The real gap is narrower: the line never crosses to the Demand panel, and no Qd/Qs readout exists before 4.b. The reviewer also frames the posted-ask/outbid mechanism as a foreign apparatus. It is Taylor's own original concept in Bx_Equilibrium_Video.typ ('let's just assume sellers post their price'; 'if someone is already at a seller, the new buyer will have to make a better offer'; 'then do the next one').
verdicts.corrected_claim: The discovery section never carries a price line onto the Demand panel and never shows a Qd or Qs readout until 4.b. The B1/B2 read-across/read-down move cannot be performed on demand, and can be performed on supply only when posted prices happen to coincide. The fix is a smaller change than implied: extend the existing common red dashed line across both panels at the settle holds and add the two readouts. One caveat applies. In these tiny discrete markets Qd=Qs holds over an interval (2x2: any P in [4,6]), so the overlay will show a range of clearing prices. $5.50 is path-dependent, as the storyboard admits at :101 and :141-143.

verdicts.title: The 4.a definition card names something students did not watch and drops the assessed half
verdicts.note: Verified: the card text is at 03_Equilibrium.py:1213 and is reused at :2008. The notes' definition is at 01_Notes.md:67. The skillsheet B3.1 wording and B5 notes :92 are as quoted. Frame 34 has no Qd/Qs, and the gold arrow lands on the dotted $4 segment of the Supply panel. 4.a at 386.5s to 5.h at 531.4s is 145s. Frame 35 shows the two-unit plateau overlap on units 4-6. Three problems. (1) The title contradicts the finding's own body. The card ('no one wants to change') names exactly what students watched, which is renegotiations stopping. It is also Taylor's original wording ('this settling down where no one wants to move is equilibrium', .typ) and the episode's bumper thesis. The defect is only the missing Qd=Qs half. (2) The equivalence gets more than 'one static frame (4.b)'. Frame 65 (5.h.iii) holds the same card beside P=$4 across the combined unit graph with Qd=Qs=6. The 5.c and 5.g settles restore P=$4 and Qd=Qs=6 (code :1865). So the fused composition already exists; it just arrives at the very end. (3) The fix is understated as a 'one-line code change'. The full notes definition is about twice the length of the Shortage card, which already spans about two-thirds of the frame at the fixed 0.7443 size. Style guide :224 requires a reflow to two lines at the same size. The suggested fixture (MC 3.5/4.5) does not give a clean crossing. MB still has two 4s, so at $4 Qd is 4 to 6 against Qs=5. It would also remove the MB-$4/MC-$4 marginal participants that 5.h selects at :1896-1898.
verdicts.corrected_claim: The 4.a card correctly names what was watched but omits 'quantity supplied equals quantity demanded'. At 4.a nothing on screen lets students see Qd=Qs. The composition that fuses both halves (card, P=$4 line across the combined graph, and Qd=Qs=6) exists only at 5.h.iii, the last teaching hold. Moving that composition to 4.a/4.b is the cheapest fix. The longer definition needs a two-line reflow, not a string swap.

verdicts.title: B3 is a structural outlier against Taylor's own B1/B2 pattern
verdicts.note: I re-aggregated both present.json files. B2 has 84 named stops and 176.4s, with 2.b at 22s, 3.n at 75s, 5.a at 151s and 8.a at 176s. B3 has 224 named stops and 547.3s. Section counts are 3.* = 128 stops, 2.a-b = 9, 2.c = 5, 4.c-e plus exercise = 8, 5.a-c = 23, 5.d-g = 41 plus exercise, and 5.h = 6. Growth-loop stops total 107. S2 alone is 47 stops from 193.0s to 312.4s (119s). 4.a at 386.5s is 70.6% of motion. There are 43 '.options' stops in growth and 49 overall. Code lines :1101-1195 are as cited. Taylor's quote at pre-restage notes :183 ('for larger scenes, we can't have the deliberation step') is real. Notes 3.a ('quick random price checks, continuous action') and 3.b describe a continuous 10x10 run that the storyboard explicitly drops at :114 ('no deferred full-market trading batch'). Small corrections. Named stops before 4.a number 144 including 0.a (143 from 2.a to 3.b), not 142. The rise from 46 holds to 224 is not all growth: about 65 of the new stops come from the back-half refinement (5.a/5.d algebra stops plus 42 round stops). Motion seconds are not class time, as the reviewer notes. B1's export has no named stops, so the B1 comparison rests on its storyboard only. Caveat on the fix: storyboard :256-266 ('visible decisions are never reduced to a single unexplained seller highlight') reads like a Taylor review correction. Un-stopping the growth pauses is safer than deleting the survey visuals.

verdicts.title: One-at-a-time arrivals are B5 comparative statics performed 17 times before equilibrium is defined
verdicts.note: Verified: the axis rescales 0-2, 0-3, 0-4 and 0-10 (frames 19, 21, 27, 34). Storyboard :220-227 is as quoted. B5 notes :37 is as quoted. Sequential arrivals are recorded as Taylor's review request at storyboard :204-205. Overstatements. (a) 'Students never see a fixed market converge to its one price' is false for the whole episode. 5.c and 5.g are fixed 10x10 markets converging from $3 and $6 back to $4. They come after the definition and with the common-price readout removed. (b) 'The final $4 reads as wherever the last arrival left things' is off. Frame 29 (S2.settled, t=312s) shows the 4x4 market already at asks of about $4.25/$4/$4.25/$4. The last twelve arrivals (74s, about 51 stops) barely move the price; most are '.declined' or empty '.settled' holds. (c) 'A given pair of curves has one price where Qd=Qs' is not true of these small discrete markets. They have clearing intervals: 2x2 is [4,6] and 3x2 is [6,7]. (d) One-at-a-time arrival is Taylor's choice in three places: notes 2.c ('We can keep adding people this way, one at a time'), the .typ ('then do the next one'), and the storyboard review. It is not animator drift. (e) 'B5 will have to rebuild it' is speculation. The same plaza could be a callback. The arrival count is 18 by my count, not 17, which is immaterial.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Before the definition, students see four or more different settle prices under one title and never see a fixed population converge. The big price move ($6.25 to about $4) is buried inside S2's 47 uncaptioned stops. Everything from 4x4 to 10x10 is economically inert for price. The notes' own 3.a/3.b, a continuous 10x10 run, would supply the fixed-market convergence. The named-cast arrivals are Taylor's design and do useful work as unlabeled shortage/excess.

verdicts.title: The shot B2 promised and B4/B5 need is missing: one price tracker sweeping the combined graph with Qd/Qs attached
verdicts.note: Verified: B2 storyboard 8.a (:142-143) describes the side-by-side shared-price ValueTracker sweep with Qd/Qs labels sliding. B3 notes 1.a/1.b plan twin graphs and a drifting price with '?'. The stop list goes 0.a then 2.a, and there are no '1.' pauses in the code. Storyboard :198-199 removes the common-price readout during adjustment. Frame 50 shows no P label and no Qd/Qs, and the title still reads 'What happens at $3?' while asks sit at $4. B4 notes :141-143 carry the oscillate-to-equilibrium cue. Overstated citations. Style guide :410 says reuse the prior animation literally 'when requested', and :341 says the 8.a device 'is not a mandatory ending'. Neither 'already prescribes' copying 8.a into B3. The B4 cue is B4's own animation direction, so B4 plans to build that device itself. Removing the common price during decentralized rounds is the honest choice because sellers' asks differ. The reviewer's fix correctly puts the sweep on the aggregate 5.a graph instead. Taylor improvises around the notes, so the B1/B2 recap may have been given verbally. Whether the missing opener mattered is unverifiable from the materials.
verdicts.corrected_claim: B3 has no continuous price sweep with attached Qd/Qs on any combined graph. The $3 and $6 reads are two static snapshots, and the return to $4 is shown only as per-seller ticks. A tracker roll from $3 to $4 and from $6 to $4 on the 5.a aggregate axes is consistent with style guide :261-263 and would carry the direction-of-adjustment skill. It is a recommendation, not something the style guide already mandates.

verdicts.title: Assessed B3.1 skills get a small, late share of the holds; two sub-skills get none
verdicts.note: Verified: the B_Skillsheet.typ B3.1 bullets are as quoted, including 'quantity exchanged as the smaller of'. Exercise_B3.typ :65 reads 'Is this a shortage or an excess, and how large?'. Code :1554-1557 draws the gap as an unlabeled Line with color=DEFINITION at opacity 0.55. Frame 45 shows the olive/gold segment with no number. Grep finds no 'exchanged' and no gap arithmetic in the code. Frame 46 shows Qs=4/Qd=8 with ringed left-out buyers and no 'exchanged' mark. B4 notes :283-285 carry the 'how much is sold? Q_S' Q&A. The stop shares are about right. One addition: B3's own 01_Notes.md never mentions quantity exchanged or the size of the gap either. This is a notes-plus-animation gap against the skillsheet, not only an animation omission. Because Taylor improvises, he may have said it aloud. The animation gives him no hold that prompts it.

verdicts.title: The simulation drifted from companion sidecar to main episode, against the original concept's own guardrails
verdicts.note: Verified: pre-restage notes :19 say 'In a companion video'. Storyboard :16-18 and :157 are as quoted. The .typ :98 and :100 are as quoted. Notes 4.e says 'exactly where the market settled' while storyboard :190-192 says the representations 'share price, not quantity'. B1 B17 has 'many thin grey bars'. But 'drift' misattributes the cause. Moving the sim to the front was Taylor's explicit 09-20 direction (pre-restage :185: 'start with the small number of players first, building up equilibrium, then do the deviations animations on the back end'). Market_Scene_Design.md is a 'Design proposal · September 9' engineering document, not Taylor's concept. 'Add decentralized repricing after these basic representations...work together' (:145) is a build and acceptance order for the engine, not a lesson sequence. Reading it as a pedagogical guardrail is a stretch. Taylor's actual concept, the .typ, prescribes posted prices, a buyer walking the line, outbidding, 'then do the next one', and 'this settling down where no one wants to move is equilibrium'. The mechanism and the card wording are therefore faithful to it. The side MB/MC panels added 'per Taylor's latest review' partly honor 'keep referencing the standard market graph'. Two guardrails were genuinely weakened. Compression did not happen (Taylor's :183 quote and design doc :60). The reference graph never carries a price across both curves.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Putting the simulation first was Taylor's deliberate call, and its mechanism matches his original .typ concept. What got lost in implementation is (a) compression for larger scenes, which Taylor himself asked for, (b) a continuously referenced standard graph with a price on both curves, and (c) any visible toy-to-line bridge at the 4.b to 4.c cut.

verdicts.title: 2.a/2.b recalls B1/B2 vocabulary faithfully but points at B4's question and skips the price experiment that poses B3's question
verdicts.note: Verified: frame 05 shows all five labels. The 2.c.accepted caption reads 'gains $7−$4.25=$2.75' (code :418). Notes :33 contain the '$2–$6 window ... Part A' sentence, and the 2.a staging comment names 'the $2–$6 window', yet storyboard 2.a.i shows only a fixed $4 offer. The B1 B12c and B2 4.d.1.price-low/no-sale/price-high price experiments exist. The first offer, the toy equilibrium and P* are all $4. The pre-restage ED note about soft-pedalling CS/PS exists, as does the ANIMATOR comment that Taylor's direction supersedes it. Overstated: 'the five labels have no later job' and 'frames the opening as B4's question'. Taylor explicitly requested this accounting ('use the price line in red to show what's going to the seller and the buyer, and expenditure, and cs and ps'). Notes 2.b gives it a B3 job: 'The price is doing the splitting: it divides the gains'. That conflict over the split is what drives the bidding in 2.c. 2.c's 'gains $7−$4.25' is CS without the name, so the disconnect is one word of vocabulary, not a reason to cut 2.b.
verdicts.corrected_claim: 2.b has a legitimate B3 job (price splits the gains, so each side wants to move it), but the animation never cashes it in. 2.c switches to 'gains' instead of CS. The $2–$6 window that the notes call for has no picture, so the question of which price in the window holds is never posed before competition answers it. Starting the first offer at the eventual equilibrium, $4, invites the misreading that $4 was given. The window/price-experiment fix and a non-$4 opening offer are sound. Shrinking or moving 2.b goes against Taylor's explicit request.

verdicts.title: The stability tests (5.h) justify 'no one wants to change' with marginal-unit logic that generalizes wrongly
verdicts.note: Verified: code :1896-1898 selects the MB-$4 buyer and the MC-$4 seller. The on-screen reasons are '$4.25 > MB $4' (:1970) and '$3.75 < MC $4' (:1995). Frame 62 is as described. The over-generalization worry is fair. The fix sketch fails under the model's own rules. In Sim/discovery.py :58 the price at an occupied seller is ask plus step. At the six-trade $4 state every $4 seller is reserved, and the four idle sellers ask at least $5 because cuts stop at MC. An inframarginal buyer's '.options' survey would therefore show $4.25 at every alternative. 'Other $4 asks available' cannot be drawn truthfully. This is presumably why the animator tested 'actual marginal participants' (storyboard :187), the only deviations that are strictly refused in this fixture. Storyboard :145-147 already disclaims stability 'against every possible strategy'. The reviewer also overlooks that frame 62 shows the seller left holding an unsold-unit box. That box is the notes' 'they would lose all their business' made visual.
verdicts.corrected_claim: The 5.h text reasons apply only to zero-surplus participants and could be over-generalized. Under this discrete fixture, an inframarginal test would not produce a refusal. The honest general argument is the market-level one the episode already owns: at $4.25, Qd=4 < Qs=6, which is an excess, so someone undercuts. At $3.75, Qd > Qs. Tie 5.h back to the 5.a-5.g machinery on the unit graph instead of swapping participants.

verdicts.title: Visual-vocabulary drift from the B1/B2 graph conventions
verdicts.note: Verified: B2's code puts white 'P' and 'Q' on every graph (B2 03_Code.py :99-100, :785-786, :912-913). B3 has none, only 'MB ($)'/'Units', 'Dollars per unit', 'Dollars per pound' and 'Q in thousands of pounds' (:564, :1243, :1300-1302). This contradicts style guide :234. The gap line uses DEFINITION (:1556), against :113 and :549. The 'Where do prices settle?' title is created at :440 and persists to 4.b. Overstated: the red claim. Style guide :149-151 makes price and selected-value readouts GUIDE red, and every red mark in the plaza is a price. The hue still means one thing. The issue is how many red marks there are, not drift in meaning. Gold bottom-question lines are in spec (:140, :144-147). A question title persisting through the beats that answer it is what :219 prescribes. The real problem is that the question gets several different numeric answers under that one title.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Two real spec breaks: the missing white P/Q axis names on all B3 graphs, and DEFINITION gold used on the gap geometry. Red remains semantically 'price'. The issue is up to ten simultaneous red marks with none dominant.

overreach: The headline and Finding 1 treat the posted-ask/outbid/walk-the-line mechanism as a foreign apparatus. It is Taylor's own original concept (Bx_Equilibrium_Video.typ: sellers post prices; a buyer checks the line for the best deal; 'the new buyer will have to make a better offer'; 'then do the next one'; 'this settling down where no one wants to move is equilibrium'). The card wording and the mechanism are faithful to the source the reviewer cites against them.

Finding 7 treats Market_Scene_Design.md, a dated 'Design proposal' about engine build order and acceptance scenes, as Taylor's pedagogical guardrails. 'Add decentralized repricing after...' is an engineering sequence, not a lesson order. Putting the sim first was Taylor's explicit 09-20 direction (_archive/01_Notes_pre_restage_2026-09-20.md:185), so 'drifted' is the wrong word.

'No single market price exists' and 'ten red marks and no the price' ignore frames 19 and 21. There the posted dashes form one red line across the Supply panel with plaza labels ($5.50, $6.25), and frame 21 already juxtaposes MB $6 with $6.25. The small-market holds are closer to a B1/B2 read than claimed.

Finding 2's title ('names something students did not watch') contradicts its own body. The equivalence gets more than 'one static frame': 5.h.iii (frame 65) shows the card, the P=$4 line and Qd=Qs=6 together, and the 5.c and 5.g settles restore P=$4 with Qd=Qs=6.

'Students never see a fixed market converge' (Finding 4) is false for the episode as a whole. 5.c and 5.g are fixed 10x10 convergences. 'One price where Qd=Qs' is false for the small discrete markets, which clear over intervals. The storyboard itself says so at :141-143, and the design doc says so at :83.

Style guide citations are stretched. :410 says reuse prior animation literally 'when requested'. :341 says the 8.a device 'is not a mandatory ending'. :219 endorses keeping a question title through the beats that answer it. Red for every price is in spec (:149-151).

Two fix sketches fail on inspection. The MC 3.5/4.5 fixture still leaves Qd ambiguous at $4 (two MB-4 buyers) and removes the marginal participants 5.h relies on. The inframarginal stability test cannot show 'other $4 asks available', because discovery.py:58 prices every occupied seller at ask+$0.25 and all six $4 sellers are occupied.
'One-line code change' for the full definition card ignores the fixed-size, 14.8-unit-width rule (style guide :224). The longer definition needs a two-line reflow.

Finding 8's 'the five labels have no later job' and 'move 2.b to B4' go against Taylor's verbatim request for the expenditure/CS/PS close-up and against the notes' stated B3 job for it ('The price is doing the splitting').

Severity and confidence run high given that the reviewer's own open questions concede the central unknown: how long Taylor actually dwelt in 2.a-3.b, and whether the recap was given verbally. Motion seconds and stop counts are proxies. Taylor's relayed remark that he improvises around the notes makes notes-versus-animation mismatches less decisive than hold-structure problems.
missed: The price story is over by the 4x4 market. Frame 29 (3.a.growth.S2.settled, t=312s) already shows asks of about $4.25/$4/$4.25/$4. The entire fall from $6.25 to about $4 happens inside S2's 47 uncaptioned stops. The next twelve arrivals (312s to 385s, about 51 stops; B6-B9 all '.declined', S6/S8/S9 empty '.settled') do not move the price. The 10x10 build therefore does not demonstrate convergence of a big market. It demonstrates that extra-marginal entrants don't matter, and no hold says so. The '.settled' holds carry no caption or question at all.

Taylor's own stated aim for the simulation is predict-then-run (pre-restage notes, Companion section): 'give enough information to predict the equilibrium price before the simulation even starts... equilibrium is predictable and about deviation... set the price, and see if anyone switches'. The current episode never offers a prediction hold. The sorted MB/MC panels are on screen for 330 seconds and are never used to ask 'where will this settle?'. One-at-a-time growth rules that out, because the final curves exist only after the last arrival. A fixed 10x10 with a 'predict the price' hold before the run is probably the missing fundamentals moment. It would also turn the side panels into the B1/B2 engine.

A unifying thread is available, and the reviewer did not connect its two halves (Findings 1 and 8). The clearing-price window narrows as the market thickens: 1x1 is [$2,$6] (the Part A window in the notes); 2 buyers and 1 seller is [$6,$7]; 2x2 is [$4,$6]; 3x2 is [$6,$7]; 4x4 and beyond is exactly $4. Showing that interval on the side panels at each named settle would answer 'where do prices come from?' as competition shrinking the window to a point. That is the Part A tieback Taylor deferred. It also makes the multiple settle prices a feature, not a confusion.

World legibility at the naming moment. In frame 34 (4.a) the six trades are a crowded cluster on the right arc with tiny red ticks. Plaza price labels were removed at the third seller (storyboard :107), so '$4' appears nowhere in the world. The notes ask for the arrow 'at the settled price' in the tableau. The arrow has to point at a side-panel segment because the world cannot show it. Market_Scene_Design.md:51 predicted this ('a forest of perspective-distorted bars'; 'quantitative comparisons should happen in the flat panel').

Law-of-one-price slippage that goes unremarked. The 4x4 settle holds two different prices ($4.25 and $4; frame 29), and the storyboard admits paths can 'settle at unequal nearby prices' (:141-143). With no spoken or visual acknowledgement, 'the price' is plural at several settle holds. This undercuts the single-price idea more directly than the red-mark count does.

Click burden as a live-teaching constraint. There are 144 named stops before the definition, 107 of them inside the growth loop, and 42 round stops in 5.c/5.g that the storyboard itself calls 'skip pauses'. Whatever Taylor says, he must advance 140 or more times before he can name the concept. Nothing in the present export marks which stops are teaching holds and which are navigation. Separating the two, for example by making non-teaching pauses non-stopping in present.json, is a cheaper first fix than re-choreographing.

Stale title during adjustment. Through 5.c.round* the title still reads 'What happens at $3?' while every ask has risen to $4 (frame 50). Likewise '$6' during 5.g. The adjustment phase has no question of its own (for example 'Which way does the price move?'), although direction of adjustment is an assessed B3.1 bullet.

The 'quantity exchanged' and 'how large' gaps sit in 01_Notes.md as well as in the animation. Neither phrase appears in B3's notes. The skillsheet and exercise Q2c therefore run ahead of both the script and the screen. This is a course-document alignment issue for Taylor, not only an animator task.

review.lens: Economics-education and learning-science literature (classroom market experiments, misconceptions, explore-before-tell conditions, animation research, threshold concepts)
review.headline: The lesson borrows the form of the Chamberlin/Smith/Holt market experiment but drops the two features that make it teach. (1) In the experiment the population of values is fixed, so convergence is attributable to incentives. In 3.a the price moves $4 -> $6.25 -> $5.50 -> $6.25 -> $4.50 -> $4 because people keep arriving. Students therefore watch about 16 unnamed equilibria of 16 different markets, which is B5 comparative statics, and never see one market finding its price. (2) In the experiment the supply-and-demand crossing is a prediction students commit to and then see confirmed. Here the merged graph at 4.b arrives with P=$4 and Qd=Qs=6 already drawn, after 143 stops of yes/no questions about single individuals. Taylor's own original plan (01_Notes_Original.md:163-175) said "predict the equilibrium price before the simulation even starts... equilibrium is predictable and about deviation". The assets that do this already exist at 5.b-5.c, 5.f-5.g and 5.h, but they sit after the algebra, from t=433s of 547s.

findings.title: Discovery act confounds the adjustment process with a changing population
findings.claim: In the canonical design the induced values are FIXED across trading periods, so the only thing that changes is behaviour and price convergence is attributable to incentives. In 3.a every arrival is a supply or demand shift and each `.settled` hold is the equilibrium of a different market. The visible price path is $4 (2.a.i) -> $6.25 (2.c.iii) -> $4.25/$4.50 (3.a.switch/counter) -> $5.50 both (3.a.two_pairs) -> $6.25 both (3.a.excluded) -> $4.50 + $6.25 (3.a.chosen) -> about $4-4.25 at 4x4 (3.a.i, t=312) -> $4 (3.b). Students see the price wander as the cast changes and then stop when arrivals stop. The fixed-population, displaced-price return to $4 is the actual Smith-style demonstration. It exists only at 5.b-5.c and 5.f-5.g, after the definition and the algebra.
findings.evidence: Holt (1996, JEP 10(1):193-203, read in full): same cards "Shuffle and distribute the same cards" each period. His fn. 5 says rotating new cohorts in is "less satisfactory, since the convergence is sometimes retarded when new cohorts enter." Storyboard lines 113 and 130: "Each arrival's responses settle before the next person enters"; 14 `.settled` stops in present.json (193.0s ... 385.5s). Frame 29_3_a_growth_S2_settled.jpg shows posted prices already about $4-4.25 at 4x4, so arrivals 9-20 (73s, 42 stops) barely move the price. Frames 46_5_b.jpg and 51_5_c.jpg show the fixed-population convergence. B5_Changes is the block that owns shifts.
findings.why_it_matters: The target fundamental is that incentives push price to where Qd=Qs. With arrivals as the driver, the most available reading is that the price depends on who shows up and that $4 is where it happened to be when people stopped arriving. That is true, but it is B5's lesson. It gives no warrant for the forces-toward-equilibrium claim that the 4.a card then makes. It also pre-spends B5: shifts are shown 16 times, unnamed, before equilibrium has a name. Davies & Mangan (2007) treat equilibrium as an integrating, modelling concept. The Economics Network threshold-concepts handbook glosses it as a resting point after shock and forces. The forces half has no clean exhibit until t=433s.
findings.fix_sketch: Reorder existing assets. Treat 2.c -> 3.a.chosen (the small named cast) as the who-competes-with-whom primer. Jump from 3.a.chosen to 3.b rather than stepping through growth; present mode already supports jumping, and 3.b is a named stop. At 3.b, with all 20 present and values visible, run the FIXED-population tests. Order: 4.b merge -> 5.b/5.c ($3 on the toy world) -> 5.d/5.f/5.g ($6) -> 5.h stability + definition card -> 4.c-4.e algebra -> Q1 -> aggregate $3/$6 calculations as application -> Q2. This is the pre-restage logical order (shortage -> excess -> can a price not change? -> equilibrium). It is also Holt's debrief order of leading questions ("who would be willing to trade more units, buyers or sellers, at a price $5" -> which way does price move -> where does it stop). Cost: construct() is sequential, so the toy-world deviation blocks (lines ~1600-1890) must be decoupled from the aggregate calculations (5.a.*, 5.d.*) that currently precede them. There is no new choreography.

findings.title: The supply-and-demand crossing is asserted, not predicted; students never commit to a market-level forecast
findings.claim: Holt's debrief makes the S&D model the punchline. Reveal the values unranked. Show the recorded price series with the curves covered ("a post-it works well"). Ask leading questions. Draw the step curves only after students grasp the balancing idea. Taylor's original plan matched this (01_Notes_Original.md:163 "give enough information to predict the equilibrium price before the simulation even starts"; :165 "others use the information to predict the market equilibrium"; :175 "then change the cards, use some math, find the price, set the price, and see if anyone switches"). In the animation the two staircases sit on screen from 3.a.overview (t=55s) but on separate axes, so no crossing is readable. At 4.b the animation itself draws P=$4 and Qd=Qs=6 under the title "What does the graph show?". Nobody was asked to say where the price would land, so the crossing confirms nothing.
findings.evidence: 03_Equilibrium.py:1225 (title) and storyboard line 156, which reveals the red price/quantity guides in the same hold as the merge. Frame 35_4_b.jpg: the toy crossing is a flat overlap of both staircases at $4 from Q=4 to Q=6. Storyboard line 148 needs "counting indifferent participants" to get Qd=Qs=6, so the picture is a smeared interval with no clear intersection point. Crouch, Fagen, Callan & Mazur (2004, Am. J. Phys. 72:835-838): students who passively watch a demonstration understand no better than those who never saw it, and those who predict first do significantly better. Holt p.6: even students with prior S&D knowledge "would not make the connection" unaided.
findings.why_it_matters: Students are meant to learn that the curves from B1 and B2 tell you where a decentralised market ends up. That only registers as a claim if the curve prediction and the market outcome are obtained independently and then shown to agree. Here the graph is built from the market's own bars, annotated with the market's own answer, in one hold. The 4.c algebra then produces $4 again for a DIFFERENT market (storyboard 157: "not a rescaling of six people"). That coincidence looks like confirmation but is not.
findings.fix_sketch: Smallest change, a one-line code edit: split 4.b into two holds. Put a pause after the staircases merge and BEFORE the red guides and readouts. Taylor asks students to write down a price and a number of trades from the picture, then advances to reveal. Better, and it pairs with finding 1: at 3.b or the jump-in point, show all ten MBs and ten MCs and collect a committed prediction of price and number of trades (paper or show of hands at $3/$4/$5/$6). Do this before any ten-by-ten adjustment runs, then let 5.c/5.g be the test. Best, and script-only: hand out the fixture `MB=[6,8,4,3,7,5,4,3,2,2]`, `MC=[2,4,3,5,4,2,6,3,5,6]` unsorted, as Holt does for watchers in large rooms (p.4: a list of values and costs plus leading questions), and let pairs predict.

findings.title: Pause questions do not meet the conditions under which explore-before-tell works
findings.claim: Every on-screen question before 4.a except one is a yes/no about one individual's choice, answerable by comparing two bar heights already highlighted. There is no student-generated product, no analysis of contrasting cases, and no chance to be wrong. The literature says those are the active ingredients. One hundred forty-three stops of watching do not create a time for telling at 4.a.
findings.evidence: Source strings: 03_Equilibrium.py:77 "Would they exchange?", :151, :385, :720 "Would Amanda-Grace keep paying $6.25?", :816 "Would Molly lower her price?", :882, :1010, then :1674, :1681, :1873, :1956 in act 5. The only why-question is :950 "Why is Gary left out?". The market-level title "Where do prices settle?" (:440) stays up from t=54s to t=386s but is never turned into something students answer. Schwartz & Bransford (1998, Cognition & Instruction 16:475-522): lectures work when learners have first analysed contrasting cases and differentiated the features themselves. Schwartz & Martin (2004, C&I 22:129-184): invention activities prepare students for the later lecture. Loibl, Roll & Rummel (2017, Educ. Psych. Rev. 29:693-715): problem solving followed by instruction helps only with contrasting cases or instruction built on student solutions. Sinha & Kapur (2021, RER): g=0.36 for problem solving before instruction, stronger with high design fidelity.
findings.why_it_matters: Phenomenon before name is the right instinct and matches Holt. The mechanism is that learners notice a distinction or gap that the telling then resolves. Questions with obvious answers produce agreement without noticing. By 4.a nothing is puzzling the students, so "Equilibrium is where no one wants to change" lands as a caption rather than an answer.
findings.fix_sketch: Script-only first. Pass straight through most `.options` holds without asking. Spend the question budget on three or four market-level commits. (a) Before 3.a.third_buyer: "MB-$8 buyer arrives, supply still two units: price up or down, and who goes home?" (b) Keep 3.a.excluded as is. (c) Before 5.c: "which way, and where does it stop?" (d) Before 5.h.i: "will she accept $4.25?". Then one static contrasting-cases table at $3 / $4 / $6 with columns Qd, Qs and who wants to change and how. Students fill it for the toy fixture from frame 46-style pictures. The table is a new but trivial asset and could live on the exercise sheet.

findings.title: Too much transient motion before the concept, and no persistent record of prices
findings.claim: There are 547s of motion and 224 named stops. The definition arrives at stop 144 (t=386s). The stretch from the 3x3 to the 4x4 market (B2 and S2 arrivals) takes 162s and 68 stops, which is 30% of all motion, for a price change of about $0.25. The quantity students must track to see convergence is the set of small red dashed posted-price marks on the supply panel. It competes with walking orbs, docking bars, rings and camera moves. Old prices are deleted as they change, so convergence has to be held in working memory.
findings.evidence: Segment tally from present.json: close-up 54s/15 stops; small cast 96s/18; B2+S2 162s/68; remaining 12 arrivals 73s/42; definition+graph+algebra 25s/10; shortage 50s/23; excess 69s/41; stability 18s/7. Storyboard 107: plaza price labels removed once the third seller arrives. Storyboard 522: "Removing a match removes both its elevated line and its floor shadow." Frame 27_3_a_growth_S2_r25_b0_options.jpg shows four red segments, a dashed MB guide, a ring, a highlighted column and docked pairs at once. Tversky, Morrison & Betrancourt (2002, IJHCS 57:247-262), read directly. Apprehension Principle: animations must be "slow and clear enough for observers to perceive movements, changes, and their timing". They are "fleeting", whereas multiple static diagrams "easily allow comparison and reinspection". Lowe (2003, Learning & Instruction 13:157-176): novices extract what is perceptually salient, especially position change, rather than what is thematically relevant. Leahy & Sweller (2011, Applied Cog. Psych. 25:943-951): long transient presentations overload working memory. Holt p.2-3: every price is "announced, and written on the blackboard" and plotted as a series (his Fig. 1).
findings.why_it_matters: Prices closing in on one number is a statement about a time series. The animation never shows a time series, only the current state. The thematically relevant change (red dashes drifting together) is the least salient thing on screen, and the most salient (orbs walking to the hub) is the same every time. Pausing itself is sound: Mayer & Chandler 2001 and Spanjers et al. 2012 support segmentation. Berney & Betrancourt 2016 (g=0.226 overall; system-paced g=0.309) suggests instructor pacing is not the problem. But segments help when their boundaries mark conceptual units, and 107 growth stops named r25.b0.options do not.
findings.fix_sketch: (a) Present-mode and script only: in class use only `.settled` stops through growth, one per arrival, or jump 3.a.chosen -> 3.b. (b) Small new animation: a persistent price-history strip (round on x, posted or accepted prices on y, one dot per trade) beside the supply panel through 3.a and again in 5.c/5.g. This is Holt's Fig. 1 and makes convergence a visible shape. (c) No-code fallback: Taylor tallies settled prices on the board as the run proceeds.

findings.title: The naming moment omits Qd = Qs; the two halves of the definition are never joined on screen
findings.claim: The notes' definition has two clauses: "the price and quantity at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded — where no one wants to change" (01_Notes.md:67). The card at 4.a, and again at 5.h.iii, carries only the second: "Equilibrium is where no one wants to change." At 4.a the arrow points to one dashed $4 mark on the supply panel. The demand panel has no price line. The two panels have separate axes, so Qd and Qs at $4 cannot be read. "Qd=Qs=6" first appears one hold later at 4.b as a readout, not as the reason nobody wants to change.
findings.evidence: 03_Equilibrium.py:1212-1221 (card + arrow target `posted_marks[first_seller]`), :2008 (same sentence reused). Frame 34_4_a.jpg: four idle buyers at left and four idle sellers, unmarked, under a card saying no one wants to change. 01_Notes.md:63-65 carries the bridging argument verbally ("What if quantity demanded was equal to quantity supplied? Here no one has an incentive..."), but the held frame gives it nothing to point at.
findings.why_it_matters: A first-year student looking at frame 34 can reasonably think those four buyers DO want to change, since they want spinach. The answer is that at $4 they are not part of quantity demanded (MB<$4), so they have no profitable move, while everyone who is part of Qd has a unit. That answer is exactly the link between the behavioural definition and Qd=Qs. It is the fundamental of the episode, and Taylor has to carry it entirely in improvised speech against a frame that does not show it. This is likely a large part of what felt slightly off.
findings.fix_sketch: Small animation change at 4.a: extend the red $4 line across BOTH side panels. Flash-count the six MB bars at or above it and the six MC bars at or below it ("6 want to buy at $4 · 6 want to sell at $4"). Dim the four and four extra-marginal people in the plaza. Add the first clause to the card. Script-only fallback: at 4.a Taylor points at an idle buyer and asks "does she want to change? what would she have to do?".

findings.title: Numbers quietly feed the 'price = fair middle / average' theory
findings.claim: Holt reports that students asked to explain the converged price "often come up with theories based on averaging all values and costs." Three design choices here are consistent with that theory and none refutes it aloud. (i) The first price is exactly the midpoint of MB $6 and MC $2, with a symmetric $2/$2 split (2.a.i-2.b.v). (ii) The toy fixture has mean MB $4.40, mean MC $4.00 and grand mean $4.20, against an outcome of $4. (iii) The exercise market P=12-Qd/2, P=2+Qs/2 has P*=7, exactly the midpoint of the intercepts 12 and 2, because the slopes are symmetric.
findings.evidence: Holt (1996) p.6. Storyboard 61, 67 ("CS $2 ... PS $2"). Fixture at storyboard 119-120; the sums are 44 and 40. Exercise_B3.typ:35-37. Only the aggregate market (intercepts 12 and 2, P*=4, not 7) discriminates, and nothing draws attention to that. Counter-evidence already in the lesson: 2.c.iii ($6.25 with MC $2) and 3.a.excluded ($6.25 with MCs $2 and $4) show price pinned by the excluded marginal buyer, nowhere near a middle.
findings.why_it_matters: A student holding the averaging or fair-split model can get through the whole lesson and both exercise questions without it ever failing. The 2.b line "the price is doing the splitting" plus an equal split reinforces a fairness reading of price, just before B4 asks students to reason about surplus.
findings.fix_sketch: Script-only: at 2.c.iii and 3.a.excluded, say explicitly that the price is nowhere near the middle of $2 and $7 and ask what pins it. Tiny code change: make the first contemplated offer $3 or $5 instead of $4, so the split is visibly arbitrary within the $2-$6 window. The notes already say any price between $2 and $6 would have worked. Handout change: give the pasty market asymmetric slopes (e.g. P=12-Qd, P=2+Qs/4 -> Q*=8, P*=4; at 5 galleons Qd=7, Qs=12) so the midpoint of the intercepts is wrong.

findings.title: Same visual mark for 'excluded at equilibrium' and 'rationed in a shortage'
findings.claim: At 3.a.excluded Gary (MB $6 < P $6.25) waits on the buyer arc with a blue floor ring under "Why is Gary left out?". At 5.b the four buyers with MB >= $3 who cannot get a unit wait on the buyer arc with blue rings under the Shortage card. At 4.a four buyers are left out with no mark. The contrast between these cases is the concept of quantity demanded. The visual language makes two of the three look the same and leaves the third unmarked.
findings.evidence: Storyboard 275 ("Gary also gets the ring at his waiting place during 'Why is Gary left out?'") and 180 ("blue rings identifying the willing buyers left out"). Frames 21_3_a_excluded.jpg, 46_5_b.jpg, 34_4_a.jpg. Frame 46 does dim the two MB-$2 buyers without rings, so the design already has the vocabulary (ringed = willing at this price, dimmed = not). It is just not applied at 3.a.excluded or 4.a.
findings.why_it_matters: It feeds the shortage = some people do not get the good = scarcity confusion. Students see people going without at equilibrium and people going without at $3, and the same ring marks both. The definition "Qd > Qs" separates them only if Qd has been tied to MB >= P, which the ring could do for free.
findings.fix_sketch: Use the 5.b convention everywhere. Ring = MB >= current price (counted in Qd); dim = MB < price. Gary at 3.a.excluded gets dimmed, not ringed. His ring was a focus cue, so a different highlight avoids the clash. The 4.a nontraders get dimmed. Then add one script-only contrast at 5.b: "Gary at $6.25 earlier vs these four now — what's different?".

findings.title: Three markets in one lesson; price is coincidentally invariant across two of them
findings.claim: The toy plaza (6 trades at $4), the aggregate spinach market (40 thousand lb at $4) and the pasty exercise (galleons) are three separate markets. The toy and aggregate markets share P*=$4 and the deviation prices $3 and $6 but are explicitly "not a rescaling". Act 5 computes Qs=20, Qd=45 on the aggregate and then shows Qs=4, Qd=8 on the toy for the same price.
findings.evidence: Storyboard 157, 165 ("The six units in the toy world are never labeled 40,000 pounds"), 190-191 ("The two representations share price, not quantity"). Frames 45 -> 46. Pang & Marton (2005, Instructional Science 33:159-191), variation theory: learners discern what varies against what is held invariant, so unplanned variation misdirects discernment. The Economics Network threshold-concepts handbook, summarising that work, says to "draw learner's attention to simultaneous variation in features critical to conception".
findings.why_it_matters: Students cannot tell whether the algebra's $4 is a prediction about the plaza they watched. It is not. Nor can they tell why the same $3 gives a gap of 25 in one picture and 4 in the next. The switch costs attention at the moment the shortage concept is introduced, and it breaks the prediction-confirmed link that finding 2 tries to build.
findings.fix_sketch: Script-only: name the switch once as a different, bigger market with the same logic, and keep each deviation argument inside ONE market. Under the finding-1 reorder this happens naturally. The toy-world deviations carry the concept. The aggregate algebra at $3 and $6 comes afterwards as the same question answered with equations, mirroring the exercise.

what_works: 3.a.two_pairs -> 3.a.excluded -> 3.a.excluded.reason is a genuine contrasting case in the Schwartz & Bransford sense. It shows the same Gary, the same MB $6 and the same two sellers; only a higher-value buyer is added, and the card puts the two situations side by side ("Gary traded at $5.50. Now $6.25 > MB $6."). It is the lesson's one real why-question. It also shows price pinned by the excluded marginal buyer, which counters the averaging theory. Keep it and lean on it.

5.b (frame 46_5_b.jpg) is the best single frame in the episode. It shows the world and the merged graph together, with Qs=4 and Qd=8 drops, rings on exactly the willing-but-unserved buyers, the MB-$2 buyers dimmed, and the name arriving after the phenomenon. This is Holt's leading question ("who would be willing to trade more units, buyers or sellers, at a price...") rendered visually.

5.c and 5.g are correct Smith-style convergence demonstrations. They use a fixed population and a displaced price, and they return to six trades at $4 through audited permitted moves. 5.g.production ("Would these sellers produce at $4?") usefully separates quantity supplied from sellers present.

The 5.h stability tests use actual marginal participants (MB-$4 buyer offered $4.25, MC-$4 seller offered $3.75). They turn "no one wants to change" into a test and are the "set the price, and see if anyone switches" of Taylor's original plan. They belong at the naming moment, not as a coda.

Building step-function curves out of visible people is endorsed by Holt ("the time it takes to explain the step-function market demand and supply curves is well spent, since this makes later explanations (for example, of consumer surplus) much easier"). That pays off directly in B4. The 2.b.iii green expenditure boundary sliding over to become revenue serves the same purpose.

The schematic visual language (orbs, bars, one red price line; dashed = contemplated, solid = accepted) fits Tversky et al.'s advice to "lean toward the schematic and away from the realistic". Instructor-paced segmentation with named holds is supported by the segmenting literature (Mayer & Chandler 2001; Spanjers et al. 2012) and by Berney & Betrancourt's system-paced moderator. The problem is the number and granularity of holds, not the pause architecture.

A guaranteed-convergence animated market has a real advantage over a live pit market. Cartwright & Cartwright (2024, JEE 55:276-291; 85 sessions, 243 markets) observed convergence toward equilibrium in only about 55% of sessions. A hybrid keeps the pedagogical core at far lower risk: students predict from the values, and the animation runs the experiment.
The excess-not-surplus aside (5.e) heads off a documented vocabulary collision with CS/PS before B4.
The storyboard's candour that the $0.25 tick rule is "not a proof of general convergence" and that other paths settle at unequal nearby prices.
open_questions: How many of the 128 stops in 3.a did Taylor actually hold in class, and how many minutes of class time passed before the 4.a card? If growth was mostly skipped, finding 4 shrinks and findings 1, 2 and 5 carry the diagnosis.

Is a 10-12 trader live pit market feasible in this room? Holt (p.4) uses a few traders near the aisles while everyone else gets the list of values and costs plus leading questions. B_Outline.typ Tutorial 2.3 says "We've done something like this in classes in past semesters". Why was it dropped for the animation, and could students be predictors even if nobody trades?

Evidence base for experiments. Emerson & Taylor (2004, Southern Econ. J. 70(3):672-693) and Dickie (2006, JEE 37(3):267-288) report TUCE gains from classroom experiments. The Economics Network handbook summarises Dickie as finding that the gain disappears when credit depends on performance. Durham, McKinnon & Schulman (2007, Economic Inquiry 45(1):162-178) report effects on performance, attitudes and retention that vary by learning style. I verified that these works exist, and the summary-level findings come from abstracts and the handbook. I did not read the full texts, so no effect sizes are asserted. All of this concerns PARTICIPATION. I found no study of spectating an animated market, so extrapolation to this design is by mechanism (prediction, fixed values, debrief), not by direct evidence.

UNVERIFIED as a documented empirical finding: the circular-reasoning misconception (price rises so demand falls so price falls) and the movement-along versus shift confusion are widely asserted in textbooks and teaching guides. I could not locate a primary study quantifying them. Strober & Cook (1992, JEE 23:125-151, 'Economics, Lies, and Videotapes') is cited by Simkins & Maier (2008, arXiv:0807.3534) as documenting students' difficulty applying basic S&D concepts to graphs, but I did not read it. If the misconception is real, 3.a's arrival-driven price changes followed by 5.x's price-driven quantity changes, with no flag separating them, is where this lesson would feed it.

Chamberlin (1948, JPE 56(2):95-108) and Smith (1962, JPE 70(2):111-137) verified. Chamberlin's decentralised bilateral wandering did NOT converge well, and Smith's change was public price information. The animation's survey mode (each buyer compares every seller) is effectively full public information. It is worth one sentence in class: "this works because everyone can see every price". That is also the third caveat in Bx_Equilibrium_Video.typ.
